derivations.claim: A corner in a compact surface with faces is isolated, so compactness gives finitely many corners. Choose pairwise disjoint quadrant charts about them; their two coordinate directions give product collars of the incident faces that agree on the quadrant. After deleting smaller corner charts, each remaining closed face piece is a compact smooth one-manifold with boundary, so [F4] supplies collars there. Shrinking them to the chart overlap and interpolating their positive normal coordinates gives collars agreeing with the quadrant collars. This finite construction gives the compatible face collars in the definition. A black face glues to an oppositely oriented black face of the same type, and the interval endpoint colors match by the stated rule; therefore the quotient retains an oriented surface with corners and the unglued free faces retain their labels.

Replacing either collar by a shorter collar or a smooth increasing reparameterization of its normal coordinate changes the glued surface by a diffeomorphism that is the identity outside the seam collars and on the residual black boundary. A boundary-relative diffeomorphism of either input extends over its product collar by the product map and hence descends to the glued quotient. Thus gluing is independent of representatives and collar widths in the stated equivalence class.

For three composable representatives, both parenthesized composites identify the same three collared surfaces along the same two black boundary parameterizations. In product coordinates, both quotients are obtained by replacing the two seam collars by the same concatenated interval; a smooth increasing reparameterization of that interval gives a diffeomorphism fixed on the exterior black boundary. Hence composition is associative on equivalence classes. Gluing an identity cylinder merely lengthens a collar and is equivalent to the original surface by step 1.2.

Ordered disjoint union is associative with the empty surface as strict unit at the level of words and diffeomorphism classes. The cylinder that permutes components gives the symmetry; composition of these cylinders is permutation composition, and its double application is the identity permutation. The interchange law holds because gluing and disjoint union act on disjoint collared components. Thus the category is strict symmetric monoidal, and [F2]–[F3] identify its required coherence data.

The condition $\partial_1M=\varnothing$ is preserved by gluing and disjoint union, so the circle-only objects and no-free-boundary morphisms form the stated closed symmetric monoidal subcategory. The excluded full-subcategory convention would admit a morphism with a nonempty free circular face, which violates $\partial_1M=\varnothing$.

For the strong monoidal functors of [F5], identity natural transformations satisfy the binary and unit compatibility equations of [F6]; if two transformations satisfy them, substitution in those equations shows their componentwise vertical composite also satisfies them. Their identity and associativity laws hold componentwise in the target category [F1]. Thus the morphisms between the functors in the definition form the stated category.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Under the definable-class convention of
[[def-language-of-set-theory]], every class below is a
formula and every function whose domain may be proper-class-sized is a
definable class-function schema. When its domain is a set, it is an ordinary
set-valued function.

A **category** $\mathcal C$ consists of a class
$\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal C)$ of **objects**, a class
$\operatorname{Mor}(\mathcal C)$ of **morphisms**, functions
$\operatorname{dom},\operatorname{cod}:\operatorname{Mor}(\mathcal C)\to
\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal C)$, an **identity morphism**
$1_A:A\to A$ for every object $A$, and a **composite**
$g\circ f:A\to C$ whenever $f:A\to B$ and $g:B\to C$.

These data satisfy, whenever the composites are defined,

$$h\circ(g\circ f)=(h\circ g)\circ f,\qquad 1_B\circ f=f=f\circ1_A.$$

We write $\mathcal C(A,B)$, or $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal C}(A,B)$, for the
**hom-collection** of morphisms with domain $A$ and codomain $B$. The object
class is allowed to be empty; then the morphism class is empty and all axioms
are vacuous.

**Morphisms carry their domain and codomain.** A category is often presented the
other way round, by saying what the morphisms from $A$ to $B$ are for each pair
of objects. When it is, $\operatorname{Mor}(\mathcal C)$ is the **disjoint
union** of those hom-collections: a morphism is a triple $(A,B,f)$ with $f$ in
the collection assigned to $(A,B)$, and $\operatorname{dom}$ and
$\operatorname{cod}$ are the first two projections, which are then functions in
the required sense. This is not a technicality that can be dropped. In this
library a function is a set of ordered pairs and does not determine a codomain
([[def-function]]), so the empty function is a function $\varnothing\to B$ for
every $B$ at once; reading the morphisms of $\mathbf{Set}$ as bare functions
would give that one set two different codomains and leave $\operatorname{cod}$
undefined. Every concrete category below whose morphisms are described as
structure-preserving maps is to be read with this tagging, and each hom-collection
is then in canonical bijection with the corresponding collection of untagged
maps, so no size or smallness claim is affected.

A **monoidal category** is a category $\mathcal C$ equipped with:

- a bifunctor $\otimes:\mathcal C\times\mathcal C\to\mathcal C$
  ([[def-product-category]], [[def-functor-and-contravariant-functor]]);
- an object $\mathbf 1$ of $\mathcal C$;
- natural isomorphisms ([[def-natural-isomorphism]])
  $$\alpha_{X,Y,Z}:((X\otimes Y)\otimes Z)\longrightarrow X\otimes(Y\otimes Z),$$
  $$\lambda_X:(\mathbf 1\otimes X)\longrightarrow X,\qquad \rho_X:(X\otimes\mathbf 1)\longrightarrow X,$$

such that the following two equations hold for all objects
$W,X,Y,Z\in\mathcal C$.

The **pentagon axiom** is

$$\alpha_{W,X,Y\otimes Z}\circ\alpha_{W\otimes X,Y,Z}=(1_W\otimes\alpha_{X,Y,Z})\circ\alpha_{W,X\otimes Y,Z}\circ(\alpha_{W,X,Y}\otimes1_Z).$$

The **triangle axiom** is

$$(1_X\otimes\lambda_Y)\circ\alpha_{X,\mathbf 1,Y}=\rho_X\otimes1_Y.$$

This page imposes no further axiom. In particular, the equality
$\lambda_{\mathbf 1}=\rho_{\mathbf 1}$ is not built into the definition; it is
derived later on this page.

A **symmetric monoidal category** is a braided monoidal category
([[def-braided-monoidal-category]]) whose braiding $c$ satisfies

$$c_{Y,X}\circ c_{X,Y}=1_{X\otimes Y}$$

for all objects $X,Y$.
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every smooth manifold with boundary has a smooth collar.

Let
$(\mathcal C,\otimes,\mathbf 1,\alpha,\lambda,\rho)$ and
$(\mathcal D,\boxtimes,\mathbf 1',\alpha',\lambda',\rho')$
be monoidal categories ([[def-monoidal-category]]).

A **lax monoidal functor** is a functor
$F:\mathcal C\to\mathcal D$ ([[def-functor-and-contravariant-functor]])
together with natural transformations ([[def-natural-transformation]])

$$F_{2;X,Y}:F(X)\boxtimes F(Y)\longrightarrow F(X\otimes Y),$$

and

the morphism

$$F_0:\mathbf 1'\longrightarrow F(\mathbf 1),$$

such that, for all $X,Y,Z$,

$$F(\alpha_{X,Y,Z})\circ F_{2;X\otimes Y,Z}\circ(F_{2;X,Y}\boxtimes1_{F(Z)})=F_{2;X,Y\otimes Z}\circ(1_{F(X)}\boxtimes F_{2;Y,Z})\circ\alpha'_{F(X),F(Y),F(Z)},$$

$$F(\lambda_X)\circ F_{2;\mathbf 1,X}\circ(F_0\boxtimes1_{F(X)})=\lambda'_{F(X)},$$

$$F(\rho_X)\circ F_{2;X,\mathbf 1}\circ(1_{F(X)}\boxtimes F_0)=\rho'_{F(X)}.$$

A lax monoidal functor is **strong monoidal** when the natural transformation
$F_2$ is a natural isomorphism ([[def-natural-isomorphism]])—equivalently,
every component $F_{2;X,Y}$ is an isomorphism—and $F_0$ is an isomorphism.

A strong monoidal functor is **strict monoidal** when the functor preserves the
unit and tensor on the nose and every structure map above is an identity.

Let $F,G:\mathcal C\to\mathcal D$ be lax monoidal functors
([[def-lax-strong-and-strict-monoidal-functor]]).
A **monoidal natural transformation** $\theta:F\Rightarrow G$ is a natural
transformation ([[def-natural-transformation]]) such that

$$\theta_{X\otimes Y}\circ F_{2;X,Y}=G_{2;X,Y}\circ(\theta_X\boxtimes\theta_Y)$$

for all objects $X,Y$, and

$$G_0=\theta_{\mathbf 1}\circ F_0.$$

Thus $\theta$ is compatible both with the binary structure maps and with the
unit map.

derivations.claim:
Choose a basis $(u_1,\ldots,u_n)$ of $A$. The map $\Theta:A\to A^*$ given by $\Theta(v)(a)=\epsilon(av)$ is an isomorphism by [F1]. Define $v_i:=\Theta^{-1}(u_i^*)$. Then $\epsilon(u_jv_i)=\delta_{ji}$, and [F2] gives
$$
a=\sum_i\epsilon(av_i)u_i,\qquad
a=\sum_i v_i\epsilon(u_i a).
$$
For the second identity, applying each functional $u_j^*\circ\Theta$ to its right side gives $\epsilon(u_j a)$; the nondegeneracy in the first variable then identifies that side with $a$. Set $e:=\sum_i v_i\otimes u_i$.

The first displayed dual-basis identity gives $\sum_i\epsilon(a v_i)u_i=a$, and the second gives $\sum_i v_i\epsilon(u_i a)=a$, so this $e$ has the required two contraction properties. If another tensor has the first property, contracting its first factor against every functional $a\mapsto\epsilon(a x)$ gives the same vector for every $a$; these functionals range over all of $A^*$ by nondegeneracy. Hence the tensors are equal. The contraction map $A\otimes A\to\operatorname{Hom}_k(A^*,A)$ is an isomorphism in finite dimension, so the tensor is intrinsically defined and independent of the basis.

To prove $(a\otimes1)e=e(1\otimes a)$, test the two tensors against arbitrary $\phi\otimes\psi\in A^*\otimes A^*$. Nondegeneracy supplies $c,d\in A$ with $\phi(z)=\epsilon(cz)$ and $\psi(z)=\epsilon(zd)$. The first contraction is
$$
\sum_i\epsilon(cav_i)\epsilon(u_i d)=\epsilon(cad)
$$
by the second dual-basis identity applied to $d$. The second is
$$
\sum_i\epsilon(cv_i)\epsilon(u_iad)=\epsilon(cad)
$$
by the same identity applied to $ad$. Since such product functionals separate tensors, the two tensors agree.

Define $\Delta(a)=(a\otimes1)e$. Then $(\epsilon\otimes1)\Delta(a)=\sum_i\epsilon(av_i)u_i=a$. Also $(1\otimes\epsilon)\Delta(a)=a\sum_i v_i\epsilon(u_i)=a$ by the second identity in step 1.1 at $a=1$. The central relation of step 2.1 gives
$$
\Delta(ab)=(a\otimes1)\Delta(b)=\Delta(a)(1\otimes b).
$$
Expanding these two equalities with the associator is exactly the pair of Frobenius identities in [F3].

The defining contraction also yields, for all $x,y,a\in A$,
$$
(\beta\otimes\beta)(x\otimes y,\Delta(a))
=\sum_i\epsilon(xav_i)\epsilon(yu_i)
=\epsilon(yxa)=\beta(yx,a).
$$
Use the tensor-product pairing $\beta^{\otimes3}$ to test coassociativity. For any $x,y,z,a\in A$, step 3.1 gives
$$
\langle x\otimes y\otimes z,(\Delta\otimes1)\Delta(a)\rangle
=\beta(zyx,a)
=\langle x\otimes y\otimes z,(1\otimes\Delta)\Delta(a)\rangle.
$$
The pairing $\beta^{\otimes3}$ is nondegenerate: in any basis its matrix is the Kronecker product of three invertible matrices for $\beta$. Thus the two tensors are equal, proving coassociativity.

If $\Delta'$ is another coproduct with counit $\epsilon$ and the two Frobenius identities, write $e'=\Delta'(1)=\sum_jx'_j\otimes y'_j$. Applying the counit identities to $\Delta'(a)$ and using each Frobenius identity gives
$$
\sum_j\epsilon(ax'_j)y'_j=a,\qquad \sum_jx'_j\epsilon(y'_j a)=a.
$$
Step 1.2 therefore gives $e'=e$. The Frobenius identity then gives $\Delta'(a)=(a\otimes1)e'=(a\otimes1)e=\Delta(a)$, so the coproduct is unique.

Conversely, suppose $(A,\mu,\eta,\Delta,\epsilon)$ satisfies [F3], and put $d:=\Delta\circ\eta:k\to A\otimes A$. With the canonical associators and unitors, the two snake composites are
$$
S_L:=\rho_A\circ(1_A\otimes\beta)\circ\alpha_{A,A,A}\circ(d\otimes1_A)\circ\lambda_A^{-1}:A\to A
$$
and
$$
S_R:=\lambda_A\circ(\beta\otimes1_A)\circ\alpha^{-1}_{A,A,A}\circ(1_A\otimes d)\circ\rho_A^{-1}:A\to A.
$$
For $S_L$, replace $\beta$ by $\epsilon\mu$ and use the Frobenius identity $(1_A\otimes\mu)\alpha(\Delta\otimes1_A)=\Delta\mu$; naturality of $\alpha$ moves $\eta$ to the first input. The left unit equation reduces the composite to $\rho_A(1_A\otimes\epsilon)\Delta$, which is $1_A$ by the right counit. For $S_R$, use $(\mu\otimes1_A)\alpha^{-1}(1_A\otimes\Delta)=\Delta\mu$; the right unit equation reduces it to $\lambda_A(\epsilon\otimes1_A)\Delta$, which is $1_A$ by the left counit. Thus both snake composites are identities.

The two snake identities exhibit inverse maps between $A$ and $A^*$ for the left and right pairings, respectively; hence $\beta$ is nondegenerate in both variables. It follows that $\epsilon$ is a Frobenius functional by [F1], and step 3.2 gives uniqueness of $\Delta$. Symmetry of $\beta$ and commutativity of $\mu$ remain the separate properties defined in [F3].

Let $k$ be a field and $A$ a finite-dimensional unital associative $k$-algebra ([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]). A bilinear form $\beta:A\times A\to k$ is **associative** when $\beta(ab,c)=\beta(a,bc)$ for all $a,b,c\in A$. It is **nondegenerate** when both linear maps
$$
A\to A^*,\qquad a\mapsto[b\mapsto\beta(a,b)],\qquad b\mapsto[a\mapsto\beta(a,b)]
$$
are isomorphisms. A linear functional $\lambda:A\to k$ is a **Frobenius functional** when $\beta_\lambda(a,b):=\lambda(ab)$ is nondegenerate. Associativity of $\beta_\lambda$ follows from associativity of multiplication. The algebra $A$ is **Frobenius** when it has at least one Frobenius functional.
If $B=(b_1,\ldots,b_n)$ is a basis of a finite-dimensional $F$-vector space $V$, then its dual family $B^*=(b_1^*,\ldots,b_n^*)$ is a basis of $V^*$. Consequently $\dim V^*=\dim V=n$.

Fix a field $k$ and write $\mathrm{Vect}_{\mathrm{fd}}(k)$ for finite-dimensional $k$-vector spaces and linear maps, with the algebraic tensor product, unit object $k$, canonical associator $\alpha_{U,V,W}: (U\otimes V)\otimes W\to U\otimes(V\otimes W)$, unitors $\lambda_U:k\otimes U\to U$ and $\rho_U:U\otimes k\to U$, and flip $\tau_{U,V}:U\otimes V\to V\otimes U$. The associator sends $(u\otimes v)\otimes w$ to $u\otimes(v\otimes w)$; the unitors send $c\otimes u$ and $u\otimes c$ to $cu$. All tensor expressions below use these maps, so no strictification is implicit.

A **Frobenius object** in $\mathrm{Vect}_{\mathrm{fd}}(k)$ is a finite-dimensional vector space $A$ and linear maps
$$
\mu:A\otimes A\to A,\qquad \eta:k\to A,\qquad
\Delta:A\to A\otimes A,\qquad \epsilon:A\to k
$$
such that $(A,\mu,\eta)$ is a unital associative algebra, $(A,\Delta,\epsilon)$ is a counital coassociative coalgebra, and the two Frobenius identities hold:
$$
\Delta\circ\mu
=(1_A\otimes\mu)\circ\alpha_{A,A,A}\circ(\Delta\otimes1_A)
=(\mu\otimes1_A)\circ\alpha^{-1}_{A,A,A}\circ(1_A\otimes\Delta).
$$
Here associativity is $\mu\circ(\mu\otimes1_A)=\mu\circ(1_A\otimes\mu)\circ\alpha_{A,A,A}$, and the two unit equations use $\lambda_A,\rho_A$. Coassociativity is $\alpha_{A,A,A}\circ(\Delta\otimes1_A)\circ\Delta=(1_A\otimes\Delta)\circ\Delta$, and the counit equations are $(\epsilon\otimes1_A)\circ\Delta=\lambda_A^{-1}$ and $(1_A\otimes\epsilon)\circ\Delta=\rho_A^{-1}$.

Its **Frobenius pairing** is $b_A:=\epsilon\circ\mu:A\otimes A\to k$. It is **symmetric** when $b_A=b_A\circ\tau_{A,A}$. It is **commutative** when $\mu=\mu\circ\tau_{A,A}$. These are different conditions: commutativity implies symmetry of $b_A$, but symmetry of $b_A$ does not assert commutativity of $\mu$.

An **S-colored knowledgeable Frobenius datum** consists of:

- a commutative Frobenius object $(C,\mu_C,\eta_C,\Delta_C,\epsilon_C)$;
- a finite-dimensional vector space $A_{ab}$ for every ordered pair $a,b\in S$;
- maps, for every $a,b,c\in S$,
  $$
  \mu_{abc}:A_{ab}\otimes A_{bc}\to A_{ac},\quad
  \Delta_{abc}:A_{ac}\to A_{ab}\otimes A_{bc},
  $$
  and, for every $a\in S$,
  $$
  \eta_a:k\to A_{aa},\quad \epsilon_a:A_{aa}\to k,\quad
  i_a:C\to A_{aa},\quad i_a^*:A_{aa}\to C.
  $$

These maps obey the following typed equations. The first eight equations are the colored category, unit, coalgebra, counit, and Frobenius laws. The two Frobenius equalities are written separately by their domains and codomains; this avoids chaining opposite-direction composites into one equation.

1. For $a,b,c,d\in S$, associativity is
$$
\mu_{abd}\circ(1_{A_{ab}}\otimes\mu_{bcd})\circ\alpha_{A_{ab},A_{bc},A_{cd}}
=\mu_{acd}\circ(\mu_{abc}\otimes1_{A_{cd}}),
$$
as maps $(A_{ab}\otimes A_{bc})\otimes A_{cd}\to A_{ad}$.

2. The left and right units are
$$
\mu_{aab}\circ(\eta_a\otimes1_{A_{ab}})=\lambda_{A_{ab}},
\qquad
\mu_{abb}\circ(1_{A_{ab}}\otimes\eta_b)=\rho_{A_{ab}}.
$$

3. Coassociativity and the two counits are
$$
\alpha_{A_{ab},A_{bc},A_{cd}}\circ(\Delta_{abc}\otimes1_{A_{cd}})\circ\Delta_{acd}
=(1_{A_{ab}}\otimes\Delta_{bcd})\circ\Delta_{abd},
$$
$$
(\epsilon_a\otimes1_{A_{ab}})\circ\Delta_{aab}=\lambda_{A_{ab}}^{-1},
\qquad
(1_{A_{ab}}\otimes\epsilon_b)\circ\Delta_{abb}=\rho_{A_{ab}}^{-1}.
$$

4. The two typed Frobenius identities are
$$
\Delta_{abd}\circ\mu_{acd}
=(1_{A_{ab}}\otimes\mu_{bcd})\circ\alpha_{A_{ab},A_{bc},A_{cd}}\circ(\Delta_{abc}\otimes1_{A_{cd}}),
$$
as maps $A_{ac}\otimes A_{cd}\to A_{ab}\otimes A_{bd}$, and
$$
\Delta_{acd}\circ\mu_{abd}
=(\mu_{abc}\otimes1_{A_{cd}})\circ\alpha^{-1}_{A_{ab},A_{bc},A_{cd}}\circ(1_{A_{ab}}\otimes\Delta_{bcd}),
$$
as maps $A_{ab}\otimes A_{bd}\to A_{ac}\otimes A_{cd}$.

5. The trace is cyclic across opposite colors:
$$
\epsilon_a\circ\mu_{aba}
=\epsilon_b\circ\mu_{bab}\circ\tau_{A_{ab},A_{ba}}
$$
as maps $A_{ab}\otimes A_{ba}\to k$.

6. Each $i_a$ is a unital algebra map, its image acts centrally on each $A_{ab}$, and $i_a^*$ is pairing-adjoint to $i_a$:
$$
\mu_{aaa}\circ(i_a\otimes i_a)=i_a\circ\mu_C,\qquad
\eta_a=i_a\circ\eta_C,
$$
$$
\mu_{aab}\circ(i_a\otimes1_{A_{ab}})
=\mu_{abb}\circ\tau_{A_{bb},A_{ab}}\circ(i_b\otimes1_{A_{ab}})
$$
as maps $C\otimes A_{ab}\to A_{ab}$, and
$$
\epsilon_C\circ\mu_C\circ(1_C\otimes i_a^*)
=\epsilon_a\circ\mu_{aaa}\circ(i_a\otimes1_{A_{aa}})
$$
as maps $C\otimes A_{aa}\to k$.

7. The colored Cardy equation is
$$
i_a\circ i_b^*
=\mu_{aba}\circ\tau_{A_{ba},A_{ab}}\circ\Delta_{bab}:A_{bb}\to A_{aa}.
$$
In particular, the reverse labels on $A_{ba}$ and $A_{ab}$ are required for the displayed composites to type-check.

A **homomorphism** from unprimed to primed S-colored data is a family of linear maps $f_C:C\to C'$ and $f_{ab}:A_{ab}\to A'_{ab}$ such that $f_C$ preserves the four Frobenius maps on $C$:
$$
\mu'_C(f_C\otimes f_C)=f_C\mu_C,\quad f_C\eta_C=\eta'_C,\quad
\Delta'_C f_C=(f_C\otimes f_C)\Delta_C,\quad
\epsilon'_C f_C=\epsilon_C,
$$
and
$$
\mu'_{abc}(f_{ab}\otimes f_{bc})=f_{ac}\mu_{abc},\quad
f_{aa}\eta_a=\eta'_a,\quad
\Delta'_{abc}f_{ac}=(f_{ab}\otimes f_{bc})\Delta_{abc},
$$
$$
\epsilon'_a f_{aa}=\epsilon_a,\quad
f_{aa}i_a=i'_a f_C,\quad
f_C i_a^*=i_a^{*'}f_{aa}
$$
for all indicated labels. Composition and identities are componentwise. For singleton $S=\{*\}$, write $A=A_{**}$, $i=i_*$, and $i^*=i_*^*$; this is the usual pair $(A,C,i,i^*)$.

For each $a,b\in S$, define the open pairing
$$
b_{ab}:A_{ab}\otimes A_{ba}\to k,\qquad b_{ab}:=\epsilon_a\circ\mu_{aba}.
$$
The cyclic trace equation above identifies $b_{ab}$ with the reversed pairing $b_{ba}\circ\tau_{A_{ab},A_{ba}}$. The equations do not impose nondegeneracy as a separate axiom: [[lem-frobenius-sewing-derived-moves]] proves that both induced maps to algebraic duals are isomorphisms, by exhibiting the two snake composites. For $a=b$, this is the symmetric Frobenius pairing on $A_{aa}$.

No equality $C=Z(A_{aa})$ is part of the definition. The Cardy equation is an additional map equality; it does not identify the underlying vector spaces or force the whole open algebra to be commutative.

derivations.claim: There are finitely many corners: the depth-two stratum of a compact surface with faces is a closed discrete zero-manifold, so its singleton neighborhoods have a finite subcover. Choose disjoint quadrant charts at these corners. The two coordinate directions in each quadrant give product collars of the two incident faces. Away from these charts, use [F2] on each compact one-face segment; shrink the resulting collars and reparameterize their positive normal coordinates to agree with the quadrant collars on overlaps. Thus the black and free faces have compatible collars. On a black collar prescribe $f=t$ at an incoming face and $f=1-t$ at an outgoing face.

Each free boundary component is either a circle or an interval between corners. On a circle use $g(s)=\tfrac12+\delta\cos(2\pi s)$ with $0<\delta<1/4$. For an interval, its endpoint values are $0$ or $1$. If they differ, use the monotone profile $g(s)=s$ or $1-s$. If both are $0$, choose a smooth function with derivative $+1$ near the first endpoint, derivative $-1$ near the second, and one simple zero of the derivative in the interior; for example integrate a smooth strictly decreasing function $\theta$ with $\theta(1-s)=-\theta(s)$ and $\theta=\pm1$ near the endpoints. If both endpoints are $1$, use one minus that profile. The endpoint germs match the black-corner collar coordinates. A smooth inward extension $g(s)+t h(s,t)$ is chosen with $h=0$ near the endpoints, so it agrees with the black-corner collars, and $h>0$ at each free-face critical point, so the full differential is nonzero there. Every critical value lies strictly between $0$ and $1$. Since there are finitely many components, choose their positive scales successively so the finitely many circle extrema and interval extrema avoid all previously chosen critical values; each scale ranges over an open interval and has only finitely many forbidden values.

Extend these prescribed functions from a smaller collar neighborhood to $M$ by a finite chart cover and smooth bump functions. On the resulting boundary neighborhood the full differential is nonzero: on black faces the collar derivative is nonzero; on free faces either the tangential derivative or the chosen normal derivative is nonzero; at corners the tangential germ is the nonzero linear endpoint germ. Compactness therefore leaves a compact set $K$ in the interior outside which no perturbation is needed. Cover $K$ by finitely many coordinate charts $U_i$ and smaller sets $V_i$ whose union contains $K$. Choose bumps $\chi_i$ supported in $U_i$ and equal to one near $V_i$. The differentials of the finitely many functions $\chi_i x_i^j$ span every cotangent fiber on a neighborhood of $K$.

For parameters $a_{ij}$ in a sufficiently small open ball, set $f_a=f_0+\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}\chi_i x_i^j$. The boundary collars and all their restrictions stay fixed. The evaluation map $(p,a)\mapsto d(f_a)_p$ is transverse to the zero section because its parameter derivatives span the cotangent fiber on $K$; outside $K$ the differential was already nonzero. Apply [F3] to this finite-dimensional family: its bad parameter set is null. The parameter ball has positive dimension, so [F4] makes the good parameters dense; in particular it contains a good parameter. The resulting interior critical points are nondegenerate, so by [F6] the restriction is a Morse function there. Fix a set $S$ of **boundary colors**. A **black boundary component** is a parametrized incoming or outgoing boundary circle or interval. A **free boundary component** is a connected component of the remaining boundary, labeled by one element of $S$. The intersection of a black and a free face consists of **corners**. A smooth structure with corners means that every point has a chart in an open subset of $[0,\infty)^r\times\mathbb R^{2-r}$, $0\le r\le2$, and transition maps extend smoothly to open subsets of $\mathbb R^2$.

Each surface representative is equipped with smooth collars of its black and free faces that are product collars in the quadrant charts at corners. A collar of a face $F$ is a smooth embedding $F\times[0,\epsilon)\to M$ restricting to the identity on $F\times\{0\}$. The collars are used only to define gluing; morphisms forget their lengths and are identified by orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms that fix every black parameterization, preserve incoming/outgoing faces, and preserve each free-boundary color. Under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, compatible collars exist: use the smooth collar theorem on each face and choose the local product collars together in the finite corner charts.

An **object** is a finite ordered word in:

- the positively oriented circle $C$; and
- intervals $I_{ab}$, for $a,b\in S$, oriented from their left endpoint of color $a$ to their right endpoint of color $b$.

The empty word is allowed. A **morphism** from a word $X$ to a word $Y$ is an equivalence class of compact oriented smooth surfaces with corners whose black boundary is the disjoint union of a parameterized incoming copy of $X$ and a parameterized outgoing copy of $Y$, with the induced boundary orientations opposite to the object orientations on incoming components and equal on outgoing components. Every free-boundary component is colored in $S$. No free boundary is required to be connected, and a free component may be a circle (a window) or an interval between corners.

Composition glues the outgoing black boundary of the first surface to the incoming black boundary of the second, component by component, using the fixed parameterizations. A circle matches a circle; $I_{ab}$ matches the oppositely oriented copy of that same interval, with its endpoint colors in the reversed boundary orientation. Tensor product is ordered disjoint union and concatenation of words. The symmetry is the cylinder with the ordered boundary components permuted. The identity on a word is its product cylinder.

Write $\mathsf{Cob}^{\mathrm{oc}}_2(S)$ for this symmetric monoidal category. Its objects include circle and interval words and its morphisms may have colored free boundary.

The **closed oriented surface category** $\mathsf{Cob}^{\mathrm{cl}}_2$ has only finite words of circles as objects and only morphisms with no free boundary at all. It is not the full subcategory of $\mathsf{Cob}^{\mathrm{oc}}_2(S)$ on circle words: that full subcategory would also contain circle-to-circle surfaces with free-boundary windows.

For a field $k$, $\mathrm{Vect}_{\mathrm{fd}}(k)$ is the category of finite-dimensional $k$-vector spaces and linear maps with the usual tensor product, unit $k$, associator, unitors, and flip. A (closed or open-closed) **2D TQFT** here is a strong symmetric monoidal functor from the indicated surface category to $\mathrm{Vect}_{\mathrm{fd}}(k)$. Morphisms of TQFTs are monoidal natural transformations, with the binary and unit compatibility equations of [[def-monoidal-natural-transformation]].
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every smooth manifold with boundary has a smooth collar.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\mathcal F:M\times S\to N$ be a smooth family of maps and let $Z\subseteq N$
be an embedded submanifold. If $\mathcal F\pitchfork Z$, then the set of
parameters $s\in S$ for which the slice $\mathcal F_s:M\to N$ fails to be
transverse to $Z$ is a null subset of $S$.

Let $M$ be a positive-dimensional smooth manifold, let $\mathcal A$ be a smooth
atlas on $M$, and let $E\subseteq M$ be $\mathcal A$-null in the sense of
[[def-null-subset-of-a-smooth-manifold]]. Then $M\setminus E$ is dense in $M$.
In particular, under Countable Choice the conclusion holds for any manifold-null
set $E$.

Let $f:M\to\mathbb R$ be smooth, let $p$ be a nondegenerate critical point of
$f$, and let $\lambda$ be the index of $p$. If $n=\dim M$, then there are local
coordinates $(x^1,\dots,x^n)$ centered at $p$ in which

$$f=f(p)-\sum_{i=1}^{\lambda}(x^i)^2+\sum_{i=\lambda+1}^{n}(x^i)^2.$$

For $n=0$, both sums are empty.

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold and let $f:M\to\mathbb R$ be smooth.

- The function $f$ is a **Morse function** when every critical point of $f$ is
  nondegenerate
  ([[def-critical-point-and-critical-value-of-a-smooth-function]],
  [[def-nondegenerate-critical-point-nullity-index-and-coindex]]).
- The function $f$ is an **excellent Morse function** when it is Morse and any
  two distinct critical points have distinct critical values.

Thus excellence is stronger than the Morse condition: it excludes repeated
critical values, not repeated indices.

derivations.claim: A closed multiplication is the oriented pair of pants with two incoming parameterized circles and one outgoing circle; its unit is a disk with outgoing circle. A closed comultiplication is the same pair of pants with reversed height, and the counit is a disk with incoming circle. For closed associativity and coassociativity, cut either composite along the two seams joining the three elementary pants. Both cut surfaces are disks with the same six seam sides and the same cyclically ordered, parameterized circle boundaries; gluing the matched seam sides reconstructs each composite. For the unit and counit equations, cut the cup-cap seam; both sides are the same annular collar after deleting the disk born and killed on that seam. For each of the two Frobenius equations, cut along the unique internal seam and then along an arc from that seam to each boundary circle: both sides become the same four disks in the same cyclic order, and the seam pairs have opposite induced orientations. Extending the boundary matching radially over each disk and smoothing inside the product seam collars gives an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism fixed on the black boundary.

The two closed multiplication inputs may be exchanged by the symmetry cylinder. The resulting pair of pants is carried to the original by the orientation-preserving half-turn that exchanges its two incoming collars and fixes the outgoing collar as parameterized; hence the closed multiplication is commutative. The same cut-and-match arguments in step 1.1 preserve the ordering of external circles, so they prove the closed algebra, coalgebra, counit, and both Frobenius equalities with the displayed associators and unitors inserted by functoriality.

For open associativity, the two composites are the two seam decompositions of one disk whose four black interval collars occur in the order $I_{ab},I_{bc},I_{cd},I_{ad}$ along its boundary; the intervening free intervals have labels $a,b,c,d$ in that order. Cutting each composite along its two internal interval seams gives the same three disks, with corresponding black edges and all four free labels matched. The unit composites cut to a disk with one input and one output interval; the removable cap is absorbed into the adjacent product collar, which is the identity cylinder relative to the interval parameterization. Reversing height gives the corresponding open coassociativity and counit diffeomorphisms. For each typed open Frobenius equality, the two cuts give the same disk with two interval inputs, two interval outputs, and free edges successively labeled $a,b,c,d$; the first seam factors through $\Delta_{abc}$ and the second through $\Delta_{bcd}$, with the multiplication seam joining the same two boundary edges. Reversing which seam is cut first changes the parenthesization but not the matched cyclic boundary word. The disk extensions described in step 1.1 give diffeomorphisms relative to all four black collars.

The two sides of the indexed cyclic trace equality are disks with incoming collars $I_{ab},I_{ba}$ and the same two oppositely oriented free edges labeled $a$ and $b$. Cutting along the product seam gives two disks; the boundary matching sends the $I_{ab}$ collar to the same parameterized collar and the $I_{ba}$ collar to itself, while interchanging the order in which the seam is traversed. The zipper unit equality $\eta_a=i_a\eta_C$ compares two disks with the same outgoing $I_{aa}$ collar and the same two free edges labeled $a$: cutting off the zipper seam on the right leaves exactly the disk for the open unit. The zipper algebra equality compares the two decompositions of the same planar disk with two closed circle inputs and one outgoing $I_{aa}$ collar; cut along the two zipper seams on one side and the single zipper seam on the other, then match the circle collars and the two $a$-labeled free arcs in cyclic order. For centrality, both composites are the same disk strip with one closed input circle, one interval input $I_{ab}$, and one interval output $I_{ab}$; the cut arc passes between the circle collar and the interval collar on the first side and on the other side, and the resulting edge words agree because the circle has no marked point. The free edges keep their respective labels $a,b$. For the adjunction equation, the two maps $C\otimes A_{aa}\to k$ are disks with the same closed input circle, the same open input interval, and empty output; cut along the zipper seam and the evaluation seam, then match the two resulting disks in boundary order. This gives the pairing equality with both black parameterizations fixed.

In the Cardy equality, the left composite first applies the cozipper to $I_{bb}$ and then zips the closed output to $I_{aa}$; the right composite applies $\Delta_{bab}$, exchanges the two oppositely labeled interval factors by the symmetry, and joins them with $\mu_{aba}$. Both are genus-zero annular strips with the two external black intervals $I_{bb}$ and $I_{aa}$ fixed and with the same two free edges labeled $a$ and $b$. Cut the left strip along the zipper seam and the right strip along the two open-pants seams. In each case the cuts yield disks whose boundary words, read from the fixed $I_{bb}$ collar toward $I_{aa}$, are $b,a,b$ and $a,b,a$ with the same seam pairings; the symmetry on the right is exactly the interchange needed to match the two middle seam edges. Extend each matched disk-boundary map over its disk and smooth at the seams. This gives a diffeomorphism fixing the two black parameterizations and each labeled free edge, so the two displayed composites are equal as morphisms.

Applying any strong symmetric monoidal functor to the boundary-relative equalities of steps 1.1–2.3 preserves the composites and symmetry cylinders by [F3]. Its assigned maps therefore satisfy the algebra, coalgebra, Frobenius, cyclicity, centrality, adjunction, and Cardy equations with the exact types of [F2]. The defining equations are separately stated in that item, so no equality is inferred from a differently typed composite.

All tensor expressions below use these maps, so no strictification is implicit.

A **Frobenius object** in $\mathrm{Vect}_{\mathrm{fd}}(k)$ is a finite-dimensional vector space $A$ and linear maps
$$
\mu:A\otimes A\to A,\qquad \eta:k\to A,\qquad
\Delta:A\to A\otimes A,\qquad \epsilon:A\to k
$$
such that $(A,\mu,\eta)$ is a unital associative algebra, $(A,\Delta,\epsilon)$ is a counital coassociative coalgebra, and the two Frobenius identities hold:
$$
\Delta\circ\mu
=(1_A\otimes\mu)\circ\alpha_{A,A,A}\circ(\Delta\otimes1_A)
=(\mu\otimes1_A)\circ\alpha^{-1}_{A,A,A}\circ(1_A\otimes\Delta).
$$
Here associativity is $\mu\circ(\mu\otimes1_A)=\mu\circ(1_A\otimes\mu)\circ\alpha_{A,A,A}$, and the two unit equations use $\lambda_A,\rho_A$. Coassociativity is $\alpha_{A,A,A}\circ(\Delta\otimes1_A)\circ\Delta=(1_A\otimes\Delta)\circ\Delta$, and the counit equations are $(\epsilon\otimes1_A)\circ\Delta=\lambda_A^{-1}$ and $(1_A\otimes\epsilon)\circ\Delta=\rho_A^{-1}$.

- a finite-dimensional vector space $A_{ab}$ for every ordered pair $a,b\in S$;

$$

\qquad
\mu_{abb}\circ(1_{A_{ab}}\otimes\eta_b)=\rho_{A_{ab}}.

$$
(\epsilon_a\otimes1_{A_{ab}})\circ\Delta_{aab}=\lambda_{A_{ab}}^{-1},
\qquad
(1_{A_{ab}}\otimes\epsilon_b)\circ\Delta_{abb}=\rho_{A_{ab}}^{-1}.
$$

=(1_{A_{ab}}\otimes\mu_{bcd})\circ\alpha_{A_{ab},A_{bc},A_{cd}}\circ(\Delta_{abc}\otimes1_{A_{cd}}),
$$
as maps $A_{ac}\otimes A_{cd}\to A_{ab}\otimes A_{bd}$, and

$(\mathcal D,\boxtimes,\mathbf 1',\alpha',\lambda',\rho')$
be monoidal categories ([[def-monoidal-category]]).

A **lax monoidal functor** is a functor
$F:\mathcal C\to\mathcal D$ ([[def-functor-and-contravariant-functor]])
together with natural transformations ([[def-natural-transformation]])

$$F_{2;X,Y}:F(X)\boxtimes F(Y)\longrightarrow F(X\otimes Y),$$

and

the morphism

$$F_0:\mathbf 1'\longrightarrow F(\mathbf 1),$$

such that, for all $X,Y,Z$,

$$F(\alpha_{X,Y,Z})\circ F_{2;X\otimes Y,Z}\circ(F_{2;X,Y}\boxtimes1_{F(Z)})=F_{2;X,Y\otimes Z}\circ(1_{F(X)}\boxtimes F_{2;Y,Z})\circ\alpha'_{F(X),F(Y),F(Z)},$$

$$F(\lambda_X)\circ F_{2;\mathbf 1,X}\circ(F_0\boxtimes1_{F(X)})=\lambda'_{F(X)},$$

$$F(\rho_X)\circ F_{2;X,\mathbf 1}\circ(1_{F(X)}\boxtimes F_0)=\rho'_{F(X)}.$$

A lax monoidal functor is **strong monoidal** when the natural transformation
$F_2$ is a natural isomorphism ([[def-natural-isomorphism]])—equivalently,
every component $F_{2;X,Y}$ is an isomorphism—and $F_0$ is an isomorphism.

For each $a,b$, write $d_{ab}(1)=\sum_j p_j\otimes q_j$ and take $x\in A_{ab}$. Apply the first typed Frobenius identity with labels $(a,b,a,b)$ to $\eta_a(1)\otimes x$. The left unit equation gives $\Delta_{abb}(x)$; the right-hand composite gives $\sum_jp_j\otimes\mu_{bab}(q_j,x)$. Applying $1_{A_{ab}}\otimes\epsilon_b$ and the right counit to this equality gives
$$
\sum_jp_j\,b_{ba}(q_j,x)=x.
$$
This is the typed snake
$$
(1_{A_{ab}}\otimes b_{ba})\,\alpha_{A_{ab},A_{ba},A_{ab}}\,(d_{ab}\otimes1_{A_{ab}})=1_{A_{ab}},
$$
where the associator maps $(A_{ab}\otimes A_{ba})\otimes A_{ab}$ to $A_{ab}\otimes(A_{ba}\otimes A_{ab})$. Apply the second Frobenius identity with labels $(b,a,b,a)$ to $y\otimes\eta_a(1)$, then apply $\epsilon_b\otimes1_{A_{ba}}$ and the left counit. For $y\in A_{ba}$ and the same $d_{ab}(1)=\sum_jp_j\otimes q_j$, this gives $\sum_j b_{ba}(y,p_j)q_j=y$, which is the other typed snake
$$
(b_{ba}\otimes1_{A_{ba}})\,\alpha^{-1}_{A_{ba},A_{ab},A_{ba}}\,(1_{A_{ba}}\otimes d_{ab})=1_{A_{ba}}.
$$
The closed object $C$ has the same two snakes with $b_C$ and $d_C$: apply its uncolored Frobenius identities to $\eta_C\otimes x$ and $x\otimes\eta_C$ and then use its two counits.
Writing $d_{ab}(1)=\sum_jp_j\otimes q_j$, the first snake says $x\mapsto(y\mapsto b_{ab}(x,y))$ has inverse $\phi\mapsto\sum_jp_j\phi(q_j)$, because $b_{ab}(x,q_j)=b_{ba}(q_j,x)$. The second says $y\mapsto(x\mapsto b_{ba}(y,x))$ has inverse $\psi\mapsto\sum_j\psi(p_j)q_j$. Thus both induced maps to the opposite algebraic duals are isomorphisms.

The trace equation in [F1] is $b_{ab}=b_{ba}\tau$. In particular $b_{aa}$ is symmetric. A tensor is determined by its contractions against all functionals on its first factor. Since the snakes make each pairing perfect, the flipped tensor $\tau d_{ba}$ has the same two contractions as $d_{ab}$; hence $d_{ab}=\tau d_{ba}$. Associativity gives cyclic invariance with all colors retained: for $x\in A_{ab}$, $y\in A_{bc}$, and $z\in A_{ca}$,
$$
b_{ac}(\mu_{abc}(x,y),z)
=\epsilon_a((xy)z)
=\epsilon_a(x(yz))
=b_{ab}(x,\mu_{bca}(y,z)).
$$
The middle equality is the indexed associativity equation, and the first and last expressions have the stated typed pairings. Transposing this identity through the snakes in step 1.1 gives the matching cyclic invariance of the copairings; explicitly it says that the two ways of inserting $d_{ab}$ before or after an indexed product have the same contraction against every product of dual vectors. Nondegeneracy makes those contractions separating, so the tensors are equal.

Pairing adjunction in [F1] is the equality of maps $C\otimes A_{aa}\to k$
$$
b_C(1_C\otimes i_a^*)=b_{aa}(i_a\otimes1_{A_{aa}}).
$$

$$
(i_a\otimes1_C)d_C=(1_{A_{aa}}\otimes i_a^*)d_{aa}:k\to A_{aa}\otimes C,
$$
$$
(1_C\otimes i_a)d_C=(i_a^*\otimes1_{A_{aa}})d_{aa}:k\to C\otimes A_{aa}.
$$
For example, pairing the first tensor equality against $u\in A_{aa}^*$ and $c\in C^*$ reduces it to the first adjunction equality; the second reduces to the reflected equality. Pair the proposed cozipper coalgebra identity against arbitrary $c,d\in C$ using the nondegenerate pairing $b_C\otimes b_C$. For any Frobenius object, the snake and Frobenius identities imply
$$

=b_{aa}(i_a(d),i_a(c)x)
=b_{aa}(i_a(dc),x)

Fix a field $k$ and write $\mathrm{Vect}_{\mathrm{fd}}(k)$ for finite-dimensional $k$-vector spaces and linear maps, with the algebraic tensor product, unit object $k$, canonical associator $\alpha_{U,V,W}: (U\otimes V)\otimes W\to U\otimes(V\otimes W)$, unitors $\lambda_U:k\otimes U\to U$ and $\rho_U:U\otimes k\to U$, and flip $\tau_{U,V}:U\otimes V\to V\otimes U$. The associator sends $(u\otimes v)\otimes w$ to $u\otimes(v\otimes w)$; the unitors send $c\otimes u$ and $u\otimes c$ to $cu$. All tensor expressions below use these maps, so no strictification is implicit.

A **Frobenius object** in $\mathrm{Vect}_{\mathrm{fd}}(k)$ is a finite-dimensional vector space $A$ and linear maps
$$
\mu:A\otimes A\to A,\qquad \eta:k\to A,\qquad
\Delta:A\to A\otimes A,\qquad \epsilon:A\to k
$$
such that $(A,\mu,\eta)$ is a unital associative algebra, $(A,\Delta,\epsilon)$ is a counital coassociative coalgebra, and the two Frobenius identities hold:
$$
\Delta\circ\mu
=(1_A\otimes\mu)\circ\alpha_{A,A,A}\circ(\Delta\otimes1_A)
=(\mu\otimes1_A)\circ\alpha^{-1}_{A,A,A}\circ(1_A\otimes\Delta).
$$
Here associativity is $\mu\circ(\mu\otimes1_A)=\mu\circ(1_A\otimes\mu)\circ\alpha_{A,A,A}$, and the two unit equations use $\lambda_A,\rho_A$. Coassociativity is $\alpha_{A,A,A}\circ(\Delta\otimes1_A)\circ\Delta=(1_A\otimes\Delta)\circ\Delta$, and the counit equations are $(\epsilon\otimes1_A)\circ\Delta=\lambda_A^{-1}$ and $(1_A\otimes\epsilon)\circ\Delta=\rho_A^{-1}$.

Its **Frobenius pairing** is $b_A:=\epsilon\circ\mu:A\otimes A\to k$. It is **symmetric** when $b_A=b_A\circ\tau_{A,A}$. It is **commutative** when $\mu=\mu\circ\tau_{A,A}$. These are different conditions: commutativity implies symmetry of $b_A$, but symmetry of $b_A$ does not assert commutativity of $\mu$.

An **S-colored knowledgeable Frobenius datum** consists of:

- a commutative Frobenius object $(C,\mu_C,\eta_C,\Delta_C,\epsilon_C)$;
- a finite-dimensional vector space $A_{ab}$ for every ordered pair $a,b\in S$;
- maps, for every $a,b,c\in S$,
  $$
  \mu_{abc}:A_{ab}\otimes A_{bc}\to A_{ac},\quad
  \Delta_{abc}:A_{ac}\to A_{ab}\otimes A_{bc},
  $$
  and, for every $a\in S$,
  $$
  \eta_a:k\to A_{aa},\quad \epsilon_a:A_{aa}\to k,\quad
  i_a:C\to A_{aa},\quad i_a^*:A_{aa}\to C.
  $$

These maps obey the following typed equations. The first eight equations are the colored category, unit, coalgebra, counit, and Frobenius laws. The two Frobenius equalities are written separately by their domains and codomains; this avoids chaining opposite-direction composites into one equation.

1. For $a,b,c,d\in S$, associativity is
$$
\mu_{abd}\circ(1_{A_{ab}}\otimes\mu_{bcd})\circ\alpha_{A_{ab},A_{bc},A_{cd}}
=\mu_{acd}\circ(\mu_{abc}\otimes1_{A_{cd}}),
$$
as maps $(A_{ab}\otimes A_{bc})\otimes A_{cd}\to A_{ad}$.

2. The left and right units are
$$
\mu_{aab}\circ(\eta_a\otimes1_{A_{ab}})=\lambda_{A_{ab}},
\qquad
\mu_{abb}\circ(1_{A_{ab}}\otimes\eta_b)=\rho_{A_{ab}}.
$$

3. Coassociativity and the two counits are
$$
\alpha_{A_{ab},A_{bc},A_{cd}}\circ(\Delta_{abc}\otimes1_{A_{cd}})\circ\Delta_{acd}
=(1_{A_{ab}}\otimes\Delta_{bcd})\circ\Delta_{abd},
$$
$$
(\epsilon_a\otimes1_{A_{ab}})\circ\Delta_{aab}=\lambda_{A_{ab}}^{-1},
\qquad
(1_{A_{ab}}\otimes\epsilon_b)\circ\Delta_{abb}=\rho_{A_{ab}}^{-1}.
$$

4. The two typed Frobenius identities are
$$
\Delta_{abd}\circ\mu_{acd}
=(1_{A_{ab}}\otimes\mu_{bcd})\circ\alpha_{A_{ab},A_{bc},A_{cd}}\circ(\Delta_{abc}\otimes1_{A_{cd}}),
$$
as maps $A_{ac}\otimes A_{cd}\to A_{ab}\otimes A_{bd}$, and
$$
\Delta_{acd}\circ\mu_{abd}
=(\mu_{abc}\otimes1_{A_{cd}})\circ\alpha^{-1}_{A_{ab},A_{bc},A_{cd}}\circ(1_{A_{ab}}\otimes\Delta_{bcd}),
$$
as maps $A_{ab}\otimes A_{bd}\to A_{ac}\otimes A_{cd}$.

5. The trace is cyclic across opposite colors:
$$
\epsilon_a\circ\mu_{aba}
=\epsilon_b\circ\mu_{bab}\circ\tau_{A_{ab},A_{ba}}
$$
as maps $A_{ab}\otimes A_{ba}\to k$.

6. Each $i_a$ is a unital algebra map, its image acts centrally on each $A_{ab}$, and $i_a^*$ is pairing-adjoint to $i_a$:
$$
\mu_{aaa}\circ(i_a\otimes i_a)=i_a\circ\mu_C,\qquad
\eta_a=i_a\circ\eta_C,
$$
$$
\mu_{aab}\circ(i_a\otimes1_{A_{ab}})
=\mu_{abb}\circ\tau_{A_{bb},A_{ab}}\circ(i_b\otimes1_{A_{ab}})
$$
as maps $C\otimes A_{ab}\to A_{ab}$, and
$$
\epsilon_C\circ\mu_C\circ(1_C\otimes i_a^*)
=\epsilon_a\circ\mu_{aaa}\circ(i_a\otimes1_{A_{aa}})
$$
as maps $C\otimes A_{aa}\to k$.

$$
i_a\circ i_b^*
=\mu_{aba}\circ\tau_{A_{ba},A_{ab}}\circ\Delta_{bab}:A_{bb}\to A_{aa}.
$$
In particular, the reverse labels on $A_{ba}$ and $A_{ab}$ are required for the displayed composites to type-check.

\epsilon'_C f_C=\epsilon_C,

f_{aa}\eta_a=\eta'_a,\quad
\Delta'_{abc}f_{ac}=(f_{ab}\otimes f_{bc})\Delta_{abc},

f_{aa}i_a=i'_a f_C,\quad

Fix a set $S$ of **boundary colors**. A **black boundary component** is a parametrized incoming or outgoing boundary circle or interval. A **free boundary component** is a connected component of the remaining boundary, labeled by one element of $S$. The intersection of a black and a free face consists of **corners**. A smooth structure with corners means that every point has a chart in an open subset of $[0,\infty)^r\times\mathbb R^{2-r}$, $0\le r\le2$, and transition maps extend smoothly to open subsets of $\mathbb R^2$.

Each surface representative is equipped with smooth collars of its black and free faces that are product collars in the quadrant charts at corners. A collar of a face $F$ is a smooth embedding $F\times[0,\epsilon)\to M$ restricting to the identity on $F\times\{0\}$. The collars are used only to define gluing; morphisms forget their lengths and are identified by orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms that fix every black parameterization, preserve incoming/outgoing faces, and preserve each free-boundary color. Under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, compatible collars exist: use the smooth collar theorem on each face and choose the local product collars together in the finite corner charts.

An **object** is a finite ordered word in:

- the positively oriented circle $C$; and
- intervals $I_{ab}$, for $a,b\in S$, oriented from their left endpoint of color $a$ to their right endpoint of color $b$.

The empty word is allowed. A **morphism** from a word $X$ to a word $Y$ is an equivalence class of compact oriented smooth surfaces with corners whose black boundary is the disjoint union of a parameterized incoming copy of $X$ and a parameterized outgoing copy of $Y$, with the induced boundary orientations opposite to the object orientations on incoming components and equal on outgoing components. Every free-boundary component is colored in $S$. No free boundary is required to be connected, and a free component may be a circle (a window) or an interval between corners.

Composition glues the outgoing black boundary of the first surface to the incoming black boundary of the second, component by component, using the fixed parameterizations. A circle matches a circle; $I_{ab}$ matches the oppositely oriented copy of that same interval, with its endpoint colors in the reversed boundary orientation. Tensor product is ordered disjoint union and concatenation of words. The symmetry is the cylinder with the ordered boundary components permuted. The identity on a word is its product cylinder.

Write $\mathsf{Cob}^{\mathrm{oc}}_2(S)$ for this symmetric monoidal category. Its objects include circle and interval words and its morphisms may have colored free boundary.

The **closed oriented surface category** $\mathsf{Cob}^{\mathrm{cl}}_2$ has only finite words of circles as objects and only morphisms with no free boundary at all. It is not the full subcategory of $\mathsf{Cob}^{\mathrm{oc}}_2(S)$ on circle words: that full subcategory would also contain circle-to-circle surfaces with free-boundary windows.

For a field $k$, $\mathrm{Vect}_{\mathrm{fd}}(k)$ is the category of finite-dimensional $k$-vector spaces and linear maps with the usual tensor product, unit $k$, associator, unitors, and flip. A (closed or open-closed) **2D TQFT** here is a strong symmetric monoidal functor from the indicated surface category to $\mathrm{Vect}_{\mathrm{fd}}(k)$. Morphisms of TQFTs are monoidal natural transformations, with the binary and unit compatibility equations of [[def-monoidal-natural-transformation]].

Fix a field $k$ and write $\mathrm{Vect}_{\mathrm{fd}}(k)$ for finite-dimensional $k$-vector spaces and linear maps, with the algebraic tensor product, unit object $k$, canonical associator $\alpha_{U,V,W}: (U\otimes V)\otimes W\to U\otimes(V\otimes W)$, unitors $\lambda_U:k\otimes U\to U$ and $\rho_U:U\otimes k\to U$, and flip $\tau_{U,V}:U\otimes V\to V\otimes U$. The associator sends $(u\otimes v)\otimes w$ to $u\otimes(v\otimes w)$; the unitors send $c\otimes u$ and $u\otimes c$ to $cu$. All tensor expressions below use these maps, so no strictification is implicit.

A **Frobenius object** in $\mathrm{Vect}_{\mathrm{fd}}(k)$ is a finite-dimensional vector space $A$ and linear maps
$$
\mu:A\otimes A\to A,\qquad \eta:k\to A,\qquad
\Delta:A\to A\otimes A,\qquad \epsilon:A\to k
$$
such that $(A,\mu,\eta)$ is a unital associative algebra, $(A,\Delta,\epsilon)$ is a counital coassociative coalgebra, and the two Frobenius identities hold:
$$
\Delta\circ\mu
=(1_A\otimes\mu)\circ\alpha_{A,A,A}\circ(\Delta\otimes1_A)
=(\mu\otimes1_A)\circ\alpha^{-1}_{A,A,A}\circ(1_A\otimes\Delta).
$$
Here associativity is $\mu\circ(\mu\otimes1_A)=\mu\circ(1_A\otimes\mu)\circ\alpha_{A,A,A}$, and the two unit equations use $\lambda_A,\rho_A$. Coassociativity is $\alpha_{A,A,A}\circ(\Delta\otimes1_A)\circ\Delta=(1_A\otimes\Delta)\circ\Delta$, and the counit equations are $(\epsilon\otimes1_A)\circ\Delta=\lambda_A^{-1}$ and $(1_A\otimes\epsilon)\circ\Delta=\rho_A^{-1}$.

Its **Frobenius pairing** is $b_A:=\epsilon\circ\mu:A\otimes A\to k$. It is **symmetric** when $b_A=b_A\circ\tau_{A,A}$. It is **commutative** when $\mu=\mu\circ\tau_{A,A}$. These are different conditions: commutativity implies symmetry of $b_A$, but symmetry of $b_A$ does not assert commutativity of $\mu$.

An **S-colored knowledgeable Frobenius datum** consists of:

- a commutative Frobenius object $(C,\mu_C,\eta_C,\Delta_C,\epsilon_C)$;
- a finite-dimensional vector space $A_{ab}$ for every ordered pair $a,b\in S$;
- maps, for every $a,b,c\in S$,
  $$
  \mu_{abc}:A_{ab}\otimes A_{bc}\to A_{ac},\quad
  \Delta_{abc}:A_{ac}\to A_{ab}\otimes A_{bc},
  $$
  and, for every $a\in S$,
  $$
  \eta_a:k\to A_{aa},\quad \epsilon_a:A_{aa}\to k,\quad
  i_a:C\to A_{aa},\quad i_a^*:A_{aa}\to C.
  $$

These maps obey the following typed equations. The first eight equations are the colored category, unit, coalgebra, counit, and Frobenius laws. The two Frobenius equalities are written separately by their domains and codomains; this avoids chaining opposite-direction composites into one equation.

1. For $a,b,c,d\in S$, associativity is
$$
\mu_{abd}\circ(1_{A_{ab}}\otimes\mu_{bcd})\circ\alpha_{A_{ab},A_{bc},A_{cd}}
=\mu_{acd}\circ(\mu_{abc}\otimes1_{A_{cd}}),
$$
as maps $(A_{ab}\otimes A_{bc})\otimes A_{cd}\to A_{ad}$.

2. The left and right units are
$$
\mu_{aab}\circ(\eta_a\otimes1_{A_{ab}})=\lambda_{A_{ab}},
\qquad
\mu_{abb}\circ(1_{A_{ab}}\otimes\eta_b)=\rho_{A_{ab}}.
$$

3. Coassociativity and the two counits are
$$
\alpha_{A_{ab},A_{bc},A_{cd}}\circ(\Delta_{abc}\otimes1_{A_{cd}})\circ\Delta_{acd}
=(1_{A_{ab}}\otimes\Delta_{bcd})\circ\Delta_{abd},
$$
$$
(\epsilon_a\otimes1_{A_{ab}})\circ\Delta_{aab}=\lambda_{A_{ab}}^{-1},
\qquad
(1_{A_{ab}}\otimes\epsilon_b)\circ\Delta_{abb}=\rho_{A_{ab}}^{-1}.
$$

4. The two typed Frobenius identities are
$$
\Delta_{abd}\circ\mu_{acd}
=(1_{A_{ab}}\otimes\mu_{bcd})\circ\alpha_{A_{ab},A_{bc},A_{cd}}\circ(\Delta_{abc}\otimes1_{A_{cd}}),
$$
as maps $A_{ac}\otimes A_{cd}\to A_{ab}\otimes A_{bd}$, and
$$
\Delta_{acd}\circ\mu_{abd}
=(\mu_{abc}\otimes1_{A_{cd}})\circ\alpha^{-1}_{A_{ab},A_{bc},A_{cd}}\circ(1_{A_{ab}}\otimes\Delta_{bcd}),
$$
as maps $A_{ab}\otimes A_{bd}\to A_{ac}\otimes A_{cd}$.

5. The trace is cyclic across opposite colors:
$$
\epsilon_a\circ\mu_{aba}
=\epsilon_b\circ\mu_{bab}\circ\tau_{A_{ab},A_{ba}}
$$
as maps $A_{ab}\otimes A_{ba}\to k$.

6. Each $i_a$ is a unital algebra map, its image acts centrally on each $A_{ab}$, and $i_a^*$ is pairing-adjoint to $i_a$:
$$
\mu_{aaa}\circ(i_a\otimes i_a)=i_a\circ\mu_C,\qquad
\eta_a=i_a\circ\eta_C,
$$
$$
\mu_{aab}\circ(i_a\otimes1_{A_{ab}})
=\mu_{abb}\circ\tau_{A_{bb},A_{ab}}\circ(i_b\otimes1_{A_{ab}})
$$
as maps $C\otimes A_{ab}\to A_{ab}$, and
$$
\epsilon_C\circ\mu_C\circ(1_C\otimes i_a^*)
=\epsilon_a\circ\mu_{aaa}\circ(i_a\otimes1_{A_{aa}})
$$
as maps $C\otimes A_{aa}\to k$.

7. The colored Cardy equation is
$$
i_a\circ i_b^*
=\mu_{aba}\circ\tau_{A_{ba},A_{ab}}\circ\Delta_{bab}:A_{bb}\to A_{aa}.
$$
In particular, the reverse labels on $A_{ba}$ and $A_{ab}$ are required for the displayed composites to type-check.

A **homomorphism** from unprimed to primed S-colored data is a family of linear maps $f_C:C\to C'$ and $f_{ab}:A_{ab}\to A'_{ab}$ such that $f_C$ preserves the four Frobenius maps on $C$:
$$
\mu'_C(f_C\otimes f_C)=f_C\mu_C,\quad f_C\eta_C=\eta'_C,\quad
\Delta'_C f_C=(f_C\otimes f_C)\Delta_C,\quad
\epsilon'_C f_C=\epsilon_C,
$$
and
$$
\mu'_{abc}(f_{ab}\otimes f_{bc})=f_{ac}\mu_{abc},\quad
f_{aa}\eta_a=\eta'_a,\quad
\Delta'_{abc}f_{ac}=(f_{ab}\otimes f_{bc})\Delta_{abc},
$$
$$
\epsilon'_a f_{aa}=\epsilon_a,\quad
f_{aa}i_a=i'_a f_C,\quad
f_C i_a^*=i_a^{*'}f_{aa}
$$
for all indicated labels. Composition and identities are componentwise. For singleton $S=\{*\}$, write $A=A_{**}$, $i=i_*$, and $i^*=i_*^*$; this is the usual pair $(A,C,i,i^*)$.

For each $a,b\in S$, define the open pairing
$$
b_{ab}:A_{ab}\otimes A_{ba}\to k,\qquad b_{ab}:=\epsilon_a\circ\mu_{aba}.
$$
The cyclic trace equation above identifies $b_{ab}$ with the reversed pairing $b_{ba}\circ\tau_{A_{ab},A_{ba}}$. The equations do not impose nondegeneracy as a separate axiom: [[lem-frobenius-sewing-derived-moves]] proves that both induced maps to algebraic duals are isomorphisms, by exhibiting the two snake composites. For $a=b$, this is the symmetric Frobenius pairing on $A_{aa}$.

No equality $C=Z(A_{aa})$ is part of the definition. The Cardy equation is an additional map equality; it does not identify the underlying vector spaces or force the whole open algebra to be commutative.

For S-colored knowledgeable data of [[def-frobenius-object-and-knowledgeable-sewing-data]], all of the following identities follow from its typed equations: open and closed evaluation/coevaluation snakes; symmetry and cyclic invariance of the pairings and their adjoint copairings; both zipper/cozipper pairing and copairing transports; coalgebra and counit preservation by each cozipper; sliding of closed-window and handle operators; the Cardy reduction of an open handle through the closed sector; and cyclic rotation of an open product followed by a cozipper. In particular, define
$$
b_{ab}:=\epsilon_a\mu_{aba}:A_{ab}\otimes A_{ba}\to k,
\qquad d_{ab}:=\Delta_{aba}\eta_a:k\to A_{ab}\otimes A_{ba}.
$$
Both maps to algebraic duals induced by $b_{ab}$ and $b_{ba}$ are isomorphisms. With $b_C=\epsilon_C\mu_C$, $d_C=\Delta_C\eta_C$, $W_a=i_a^*i_a:C\to C$, $H=\mu_C\Delta_C:C\to C$, and $O_a=\mu_{aaa}\Delta_{aaa}:A_{aa}\to A_{aa}$, the typed consequences include
$$
\Delta_Ci_a^*=(i_a^*\otimes i_a^*)\Delta_{aaa},\qquad
\epsilon_Ci_a^*=\epsilon_a,\qquad
i_a^*O_a=W_ai_a^*.
$$
The lemma is algebraic: it assumes the relations already proved in [[lem-elementary-surface-sewing-relations]] and uses no diagram as a proof.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $M$ be a compact oriented smooth surface with black incoming/outgoing boundary, colored free boundary, and compatible corner collars as in [[def-oriented-open-closed-surface-category]]. There is a smooth function $f:M\to[0,1]$ such that:

- $f^{-1}(0)$ is exactly the incoming black boundary and $f^{-1}(1)$ is exactly the outgoing black boundary; an absent incoming or outgoing boundary is the empty level;
- near each black face, $f$ is its inward collar coordinate or one minus that coordinate, so it has no relative critical point there;
- on each free boundary face, the restriction is a Morse function with no critical point at a corner, and the normal derivative is nonzero at each of its critical points;
- each interior critical point is nondegenerate, and all interior and free-face critical values are distinct.

Cutting $M$ at regular levels between its finitely many critical values expresses its morphism as a finite composite of identity cylinders and the following ten boundary-relative cobordisms, with each local color retained:
$$
\begin{array}{ll}
\mu_C:C\otimes C\to C,& \eta_C:\varnothing\to C,\\
\Delta_C:C\to C\otimes C,& \epsilon_C:C\to\varnothing,\\
\mu_{abc}:I_{ab}\otimes I_{bc}\to I_{ac},&
\eta_a:\varnothing\to I_{aa},\\
\Delta_{abc}:I_{ac}\to I_{ab}\otimes I_{bc},&
\epsilon_a:I_{aa}\to\varnothing,\\
i_a:C\to I_{aa},&i_a^*:I_{aa}\to C .
\end{array}
$$
Here a **regular level** is a level at which the interior differential and every free-face tangential derivative are nonzero. A **critical index** is the number of negative squares in the interior Morse normal form, or $0$ for a free-face minimum and $1$ for a free-face maximum.

derivations.claim: Use the snakes in [F4] to bend each outgoing interval into an incoming interval with the reversed endpoint order and each incoming circle into an outgoing circle. Bending back cancels the inserted pairing and copairing, so it preserves the relative surface class and every marked slot. By [F2], the resulting connected surface has a finite expression in the ten generators. Regard it as a finite directed expression tree, ignore identity strands, and assign height $0$ to a source or unit; at a binary vertex define the height to be the sum of the two input heights plus $1$. Let $G$ be the number of generator vertices in the expression. Then each upstream height is an integer between $0$ and $G$.

A local rewrite below either removes a distinguished generator, strictly raises or lowers its upstream height, or moves it by a relation without changing $G$. A phase that strictly raises height terminates because the height remains at most $G$; a phase that strictly lowers height terminates because height is a nonnegative integer. When a phase removes a generator, the finite number of generators supplies the outer induction. All rewrites are instances of [F3] or [F4], so they are equality-preserving and keep the endpoint colors on every seam.

**Stage I: remove open units and counits.** Replace every open unit by $i_a\eta_C$ using equation 6 of [F1], and replace every open counit by $\epsilon_Ci_a^*$ using cozipper counit preservation in [F4]. These replacements remove the corresponding open cup/cap and replace it with a closed generator and a zipper/cozipper; no open unit or counit remains. The number of open extrema strictly decreases at each replacement, so the process stops after finitely many occurrences.

**Stage II: normalize each open comultiplication.** Fix one occurrence of $\Delta_{abc}$. Its two output legs have only the finitely many possible immediate neighbors among the generators of [F2]; cases ending in an open cap or at an exterior closed-only target have already been excluded by Stage I and the bent boundary convention. If a leg meets a cozipper, use the two cozipper/copairing transports of [F4] to move the cozipper past the coproduct; if the resulting pair of open legs closes through a zipper, apply Cardy and remove the marked coproduct. If a leg meets a zipper, use the reflected zipper transport and the two snake cancellations in [F4]. If an output leg enters an open multiplication, apply the left or right typed Frobenius equation, according to which of the two output legs enters it, to move the multiplication below the marked coproduct; if this gives two legs entering a common multiplication, use the open handle/window rotation and Cardy move to remove the coproduct. If a colored open window occurs on either leg, slide it to the opposite side by the open-window identity in [F4] and then apply the preceding cozipper or Frobenius case. These are the five local cases: cozipper transport, zipper/Cardy cancellation, the two distinct left/right Frobenius attachments, and either-side window transport. Every remaining configuration is one of the three reduced forms obtained by repeating those cases: a coproduct immediately above a reconverging open product, a coproduct with one branch in a cozipper/product chain and the other in a free open branch, or the terminal open-coproduct tail. In each residual form, every further move either removes the marked coproduct or strictly lowers its upstream height. The height bound in step 1.1 proves that the stage terminates with every open coproduct in a reduced form.

**Stage III: normalize open multiplications, cozipper sources, and open windows.** Fix an open multiplication. Apply indexed associativity to reassociate the finite chain above it; each reassociation either removes the marked product or increases its height, and no move adds a generator. Use the open-window slide to move any colored window above the product to the other side, recording its color. Replace adjacent zippers by one zipper using the algebra-map equation; transport any cozipper at the source through a product using the pairing/coproduct identities in [F4]. A cozipper source is thereby reduced to an incoming interval or one open product. Each open window in a product chain is slid toward the nearest cozipper and absorbed there by $i_a^*O_a=W_ai_a^*$; if it lies on the other side, first use the reflected slide. A terminal zipper followed by cozipper is the composite $i_a^*i_a=W_a$ by definition; when the reverse composite $i_ai_a^*$ occurs, use Cardy to replace it by $\mu_{aaa}\tau\Delta_{aaa}$. Each open-window move removes that open window or lowers its height; height zero cannot be an open window because a window has a nonempty open input/output incidence. The bounded-height argument from step 1.2 terminates the product and cozipper normalizations, and the open-window count terminates the absorption phase. Applying these operations to every occurrence yields the three reduced coproduct configurations of step 2.2 without increasing the total number of open coproducts.

**Stage IV: eliminate all open coproducts.** If one remains, choose an occurrence of minimum upstream height. Its upstream subtree contains no open coproduct. The normalized open products of step 2.3 leave two cases, up to reflection. In the first, both branches of the marked coproduct reconverge through the same open product/handle. Rotate the product by the cyclic cozipper identity, reassociate, rotate back, apply the copairing crossing, cancel the resulting snake, and then use Cardy; this composite removes the marked coproduct. In the second, one branch ends at a cozipper. Rotate the cozipper around the cycle, use naturality of the symmetry to restore the marked slots, apply the typed Frobenius equation and the cozipper transport from step 2.2, and cancel the snake; this also removes the marked coproduct. These are the two exhaustive attachments because any additional open product in the intervening subtree would contradict the minimum-height choice and Stage III.

The eliminations in step 3.1 can disrupt the normal configurations established in Stages II–III. Reapply Stages II–III after each elimination. Neither restart increases the number of open coproduct vertices, while the chosen elimination strictly decreases it by one. Induction on that finite count terminates with no open coproducts and with the Stage II–III normal configurations restored.

**Stage V: remove remaining zippers and package open cycles.** With no open caps, cups, or coproducts, every open product has a source among the finite configurations left by Stages II–IV, and every cozipper source is an incoming interval or a normalized open product. A zipper can therefore only lie on an open product branch feeding a cozipper or a closed product. Push it through successive open products using centrality and associativity. When the terminal composite is cozipper after zipper, it is $i_a^*i_a=W_a$ by definition; when the reverse composite occurs, apply Cardy to replace $i_ai_a^*$ by $\mu_{aaa}\tau\Delta_{aaa}$. If the branch is the reflected configuration, first rotate the cozipper cyclically and use its coalgebra preservation. Each completed elimination removes one zipper and creates no new zipper; between eliminations the remaining distance in the finite open-product tree to a cozipper strictly decreases. Thus the lexicographic measure (number of zippers, then sum of their distances) terminates. The surviving open products are exactly the indexed boundary cycles in [F5], so each becomes $i_a^*\mu^{(q)}$ with its full endpoint-color sequence.

**Stage VI: normalize closed multiplications.** Fix a closed multiplication. Its source has only the configurations listed by the finite generator decomposition: closed products, a closed window, a handle, cozipper outputs, or open-to-closed boundary-cycle outputs. The configurations with an external incoming closed circle or an unnormalized zipper have already been excluded by the bent boundary convention and Stage V. Apply closed associativity to join closed product chains; use the closed Frobenius relation to move a product past a closed coproduct; use the window slide to move each $W_a$ to the closed chain; and use the handle slide to collect each $H$. A tracked multiplication either disappears into a closed cycle already packaged in [F5] or moves above the next factor, strictly increasing its upstream height. No rewrite increases $G$, so the bound in step 1.1 proves termination. The result has only the closed-product sources and the two terminal forms that are the inputs to closed comultiplication or to an empty-boundary unit/counit case.

**Stage VII: normalize closed comultiplications.** Fix a closed comultiplication. The closed multiplication normal form of step 4.1 excludes a handle or window feeding a product in the wrong order; Stage V excludes zipper configurations. Apply closed coassociativity to reassociate the output tree, cancel a counit whenever it meets a coproduct, and slide $W_a$ and $H$ through the coproduct using [F4]. Each move either removes the tracked coproduct or strictly lowers its source height. Since source heights are nonnegative and there are finitely many coproducts, this process terminates with the closed coproducts in the output tree $\Delta_C^{[n]}$. The excluded configurations are exactly those that would otherwise reintroduce a closed multiplication into this tree.

**Stage VIII: order windows and handles.** At this point the remaining closed operators are the window maps $W_a$ and handle map $H$. If any window lies after a handle in the closed chain, the pair is an inversion. The equality $W_aH=HW_a$ from [F4] exchanges the adjacent pair and lowers the finite number of such inversions by one. No other stage is now allowed to create a new inversion. Thus finitely many swaps put all colored windows before all $g$ handles, giving $H^gW_M$ in [F5].

**Stages IX–X: settle the empty source and target cases.** If a closed counit remains, the connectedness and configurations already excluded in steps 4.1–4.2 force its source to be the empty word; it is then exactly the convention $\Delta_C^{[0]}=\epsilon_C$ in [F5]. If a closed unit remains, the same exclusions force its target to be empty; it is exactly $\mu_C^{[0]}=\eta_C$. Therefore the resulting connected composite is precisely $N(M)$, including when the component has no black boundary. Unbend the intervals and circles; the snakes cancel and restore the original marked source and target slots.

For any connected $M$, steps 1.1–5.1 give $[M]=[N(M)]$. If $M$ and $N$ have the same listed invariants, the candidate words in [F5] coincide, so their morphisms agree. Conversely, a boundary-relative diffeomorphism preserves the component partition, genus, free-boundary colors and multiplicities, and the marked cyclic open-boundary slot/color sequences by [F1]; hence equality of morphisms implies equality of those data. For disconnected surfaces, apply the connected reduction to each component and restore the original ordering by the specified symmetry maps; symmetric monoidal interchange proves the tensor formula.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Fix a set $S$ of **boundary colors**. A **black boundary component** is a parametrized incoming or outgoing boundary circle or interval. A **free boundary component** is a connected component of the remaining boundary, labeled by one element of $S$. The intersection of a black and a free face consists of **corners**. Each surface representative is equipped with smooth collars of its black and free faces that are product collars in the quadrant charts at corners. A collar of a face $F$ is a smooth embedding $F\times[0,\epsilon)\to M$ restricting to the identity on $F\times\{0\}$. The collars are used only to define gluing; morphisms forget their lengths and are identified by orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms that fix every black parameterization, preserve incoming/outgoing faces, and preserve each free-boundary color. - intervals $I_{ab}$, for $a,b\in S$, oriented from their left endpoint of color $a$ to their right endpoint of color $b$.

$$

\qquad W_s=i_s^*i_s,
$$

$$

derivations.claim: Let $T:\mathsf{Cob}^{\mathrm{cl}}_2\to\mathrm{Vect}_{\mathrm{fd}}(k)$ be a strong symmetric monoidal functor. Put $C=T(S^1)$, a finite-dimensional vector space. Thus $C$ is a finite-dimensional commutative Frobenius algebra.

The empty input and output reductions are the unit disk and counit disk; a cylinder gives the identity convention at arity one. Therefore $T(M)$ is the stated formula. For a disconnected surface, the components are a disjoint union, so the strong monoidal structure and [F3] give the tensor product formula.

If two morphisms are glued, their chosen decompositions concatenate; evaluating the concatenated generator word is the composite of the two linear maps. Reducing the glued surface to its unique normal word preserves that value by the Frobenius equations. Hence identities, composition, tensor product and symmetry are preserved. A map $f:C\to C'$ preserving all four Frobenius maps defines a component $f^{\otimes m}$ on every $m$-circle word, with the unit component at $k$. It is natural for each of the four generating surfaces by the four preservation equations; it is natural for a composite by induction on the number of generator factors, and for disjoint union by the tensor product rule. Naturality at the pair of pants and the two disks gives the multiplication, unit, comultiplication, and counit preservation equations, and monoidal compatibility forces its component on every circle word to be $f^{\otimes m}$. The two constructions therefore give inverse maps on every hom-set.

Write $E$ for extraction of the commutative Frobenius algebra and $R$ for the construction from that algebra. Step 2.2 proves that $E$ is fully faithful. statement.

countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

definable class-function schema. When its domain is a set, it is an ordinary
set-valued function.

$\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal C)$ of **objects**, a class

$$h\circ(g\circ f)=(h\circ g)\circ f,\qquad 1_B\circ f=f=f\circ1_A.$$

**hom-collection** of morphisms with domain $A$ and codomain $B$. The object
class is allowed to be empty; then the morphism class is empty and all axioms
are vacuous.

**Morphisms carry their domain and codomain.** A category is often presented the
other way round, by saying what the morphisms from $A$ to $B$ are for each pair

union** of those hom-collections: a morphism is a triple $(A,B,f)$ with $f$ in

the required sense. This is not a technicality that can be dropped. In this

([[def-function]]), so the empty function is a function $\varnothing\to B$ for
every $B$ at once; reading the morphisms of $\mathbf{Set}$ as bare functions
would give that one set two different codomains and leave $\operatorname{cod}$
undefined. Every concrete category below whose morphisms are described as
structure-preserving maps is to be read with this tagging, and each hom-collection

maps, so no size or smallness claim is affected.

derivations.claim: Let $T$ be a strong symmetric monoidal functor. Set $C=T(Circle)$ and $A_{ab}=T(I_{ab})$. Transport the images of the ten elementary surfaces along the structure isomorphisms of $T$ to obtain the maps $\mu_C,\eta_C,\Delta_C,\epsilon_C$, the indexed maps $\mu_{abc},\eta_a,\Delta_{abc},\epsilon_a$, and the zipper/cozipper maps $i_a,i_a^*$. Each vector space is finite-dimensional because $T$ lands in $\mathrm{Vect}_{\mathrm{fd}}(k)$.

By [F2], every defining relation is a boundary-relative equality of elementary surfaces. Applying $T$ to the closed and open pair-of-pants, disk, zipper, and cozipper relations gives each equation 1–7 of the data definition, including cyclic trace, centrality, adjunction, and the exact colored Cardy map $A_{bb}\to A_{aa}$. The snakes and indexed trace in [F3] show that each $A_{ab}$ pairs perfectly with $A_{ba}$; no extra nondegeneracy or semisimplicity hypothesis is needed. Thus extraction sends $T$ to an object of the stated data category.

Conversely, let $D$ be S-colored data. Assign $C$ to a circle, $A_{ab}$ to $I_{ab}$, the tensor product of the assigned spaces to each ordered word, and $k$ to the empty word. Use the canonical associators, unitors, and flips of vector spaces for the strong symmetric monoidal structure. By [F4], every surface has a finite elementary decomposition; evaluate it by composing and tensoring the maps of $D$ along that decomposition. If two decompositions represent the same surface, the normal-form reduction in [F4] relates them by the elementary relations of [F2] and the derived moves of [F3]. Those are equations satisfied by $D$, so both evaluations are equal. The assignment is therefore independent of the decomposition and of the representative surface.

The identity cylinder evaluates to the identity map by the unit and counit equations. If two surfaces are composable, concatenate their finite decompositions along the matching parameterized black boundary; the composite word evaluates to the composite of their linear maps. By [F4] it reduces to the normal word of the glued surface without changing that evaluation, so composition is preserved. Ordered disjoint union concatenates generator words, and the symmetry cylinder evaluates to the vector-space flip; hence tensor, symmetry, and interchange are preserved. The canonical reassociation and unit maps satisfy the coherence equations in [F1], proving that the construction is a strong symmetric monoidal functor.

A data homomorphism $(f_C,(f_{ab}))$ defines on each object word the tensor product of its component maps, with the prescribed unit component on $k$. The equations defining a data homomorphism are exactly naturality on the ten generating surfaces. Naturality on an arbitrary surface follows by induction over its finite decomposition: it is preserved under composition by the induction hypothesis and under disjoint union by tensoring the naturality squares.
