The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $M$ be a compact oriented smooth surface with black incoming/outgoing boundary, colored free boundary, and compatible corner collars as in [[def-oriented-open-closed-surface-category]]. There is a smooth function $f:M\to[0,1]$ such that:

- $f^{-1}(0)$ is exactly the incoming black boundary and $f^{-1}(1)$ is exactly the outgoing black boundary; an absent incoming or outgoing boundary is the empty level;
- near each black face, $f$ is its inward collar coordinate or one minus that coordinate, so it has no relative critical point there;
- on each free boundary face, the restriction is a Morse function with no critical point at a corner, and the normal derivative is nonzero at each of its critical points;
- each interior critical point is nondegenerate, and all interior and free-face critical values are distinct.

Cutting $M$ at regular levels between its finitely many critical values expresses its morphism as a finite composite of identity cylinders and the following ten boundary-relative cobordisms, with each local color retained:
$$
\begin{array}{ll}
\mu_C:C\otimes C\to C,& \eta_C:\varnothing\to C,\\
\Delta_C:C\to C\otimes C,& \epsilon_C:C\to\varnothing,\\
\mu_{abc}:I_{ab}\otimes I_{bc}\to I_{ac},&
\eta_a:\varnothing\to I_{aa},\\
\Delta_{abc}:I_{ac}\to I_{ab}\otimes I_{bc},&
\epsilon_a:I_{aa}\to\varnothing,\\
i_a:C\to I_{aa},&i_a^*:I_{aa}\to C .
\end{array}
$$
Here a **regular level** is a level at which the interior differential and every free-face tangential derivative are nonzero. A **critical index** is the number of negative squares in the interior Morse normal form, or $0$ for a free-face minimum and $1$ for a free-face maximum.

Let $S$ be any set and let $M,N$ be compact oriented $S$-colored surfaces in $\mathsf{Cob}^{\mathrm{oc}}_2(S)$ with the same marked source and target words. Then $M$ and $N$ represent the same morphism if and only if they have the same partition of marked black boundary slots into components, the same genus and colored-window multiplicities on every component meeting a marked slot, and the same cyclic open-boundary slot cycles with their complete endpoint-color sequences, together with the same multiset of genus/window data for components meeting no marked black slot. For each connected component, the common morphism is equal to the candidate word $N(M)$ of [[def-relative-open-closed-surface-normal-form]]. For disconnected surfaces the word is the tensor product of the component words, with the marked slot permutations restored.

The claim includes components with no black boundary: their data are genus and the finite multiplicities of colored free-boundary circles, and their word is $\epsilon_C H^g W_M\eta_C$. No color sequence may be discarded, and the theorem makes no semisimplicity or characteristic assumption.

Let
$(\mathcal C,\otimes,\mathbf 1,\alpha,\lambda,\rho)$ and
$(\mathcal D,\boxtimes,\mathbf 1',\alpha',\lambda',\rho')$
be monoidal categories ([[def-monoidal-category]]).

A **lax monoidal functor** is a functor
$F:\mathcal C\to\mathcal D$ ([[def-functor-and-contravariant-functor]])
together with natural transformations ([[def-natural-transformation]])

$$F_{2;X,Y}:F(X)\boxtimes F(Y)\longrightarrow F(X\otimes Y),$$

and

the morphism

$$F_0:\mathbf 1'\longrightarrow F(\mathbf 1),$$

such that, for all $X,Y,Z$,

$$F(\alpha_{X,Y,Z})\circ F_{2;X\otimes Y,Z}\circ(F_{2;X,Y}\boxtimes1_{F(Z)})=F_{2;X,Y\otimes Z}\circ(1_{F(X)}\boxtimes F_{2;Y,Z})\circ\alpha'_{F(X),F(Y),F(Z)},$$

$$F(\lambda_X)\circ F_{2;\mathbf 1,X}\circ(F_0\boxtimes1_{F(X)})=\lambda'_{F(X)},$$

$$F(\rho_X)\circ F_{2;X,\mathbf 1}\circ(1_{F(X)}\boxtimes F_0)=\rho'_{F(X)}.$$

A lax monoidal functor is **strong monoidal** when the natural transformation
$F_2$ is a natural isomorphism ([[def-natural-isomorphism]])—equivalently,
every component $F_{2;X,Y}$ is an isomorphism—and $F_0$ is an isomorphism.

A strong monoidal functor is **strict monoidal** when the functor preserves the
unit and tensor on the nose and every structure map above is an identity.

A **symmetric monoidal category** is a braided monoidal category
([[def-braided-monoidal-category]]) whose braiding $c$ satisfies

$$c_{Y,X}\circ c_{X,Y}=1_{X\otimes Y}$$

for all objects $X,Y$.

Let $F,G:\mathcal C\to\mathcal D$ be lax monoidal functors
([[def-lax-strong-and-strict-monoidal-functor]]).
A **monoidal natural transformation** $\theta:F\Rightarrow G$ is a natural
transformation ([[def-natural-transformation]]) such that

$$\theta_{X\otimes Y}\circ F_{2;X,Y}=G_{2;X,Y}\circ(\theta_X\boxtimes\theta_Y)$$

for all objects $X,Y$, and

$$G_0=\theta_{\mathbf 1}\circ F_0.$$

Thus $\theta$ is compatible both with the binary structure maps and with the
unit map.

Fix a field $k$ and write $\mathrm{Vect}_{\mathrm{fd}}(k)$ for finite-dimensional $k$-vector spaces and linear maps, with the algebraic tensor product, unit object $k$, canonical associator $\alpha_{U,V,W}: (U\otimes V)\otimes W\to U\otimes(V\otimes W)$, unitors $\lambda_U:k\otimes U\to U$ and $\rho_U:U\otimes k\to U$, and flip $\tau_{U,V}:U\otimes V\to V\otimes U$. The associator sends $(u\otimes v)\otimes w$ to $u\otimes(v\otimes w)$; the unitors send $c\otimes u$ and $u\otimes c$ to $cu$. All tensor expressions below use these maps, so no strictification is implicit.

A **Frobenius object** in $\mathrm{Vect}_{\mathrm{fd}}(k)$ is a finite-dimensional vector space $A$ and linear maps
$$
\mu:A\otimes A\to A,\qquad \eta:k\to A,\qquad
\Delta:A\to A\otimes A,\qquad \epsilon:A\to k
$$
such that $(A,\mu,\eta)$ is a unital associative algebra, $(A,\Delta,\epsilon)$ is a counital coassociative coalgebra, and the two Frobenius identities hold:
$$
\Delta\circ\mu
=(1_A\otimes\mu)\circ\alpha_{A,A,A}\circ(\Delta\otimes1_A)
=(\mu\otimes1_A)\circ\alpha^{-1}_{A,A,A}\circ(1_A\otimes\Delta).
$$
Here associativity is $\mu\circ(\mu\otimes1_A)=\mu\circ(1_A\otimes\mu)\circ\alpha_{A,A,A}$, and the two unit equations use $\lambda_A,\rho_A$. Coassociativity is $\alpha_{A,A,A}\circ(\Delta\otimes1_A)\circ\Delta=(1_A\otimes\Delta)\circ\Delta$, and the counit equations are $(\epsilon\otimes1_A)\circ\Delta=\lambda_A^{-1}$ and $(1_A\otimes\epsilon)\circ\Delta=\rho_A^{-1}$.

Its **Frobenius pairing** is $b_A:=\epsilon\circ\mu:A\otimes A\to k$. It is **symmetric** when $b_A=b_A\circ\tau_{A,A}$. It is **commutative** when $\mu=\mu\circ\tau_{A,A}$. These are different conditions: commutativity implies symmetry of $b_A$, but symmetry of $b_A$ does not assert commutativity of $\mu$.

An **S-colored knowledgeable Frobenius datum** consists of:

- a commutative Frobenius object $(C,\mu_C,\eta_C,\Delta_C,\epsilon_C)$;
- a finite-dimensional vector space $A_{ab}$ for every ordered pair $a,b\in S$;
- maps, for every $a,b,c\in S$,
  $$
  \mu_{abc}:A_{ab}\otimes A_{bc}\to A_{ac},\quad
  \Delta_{abc}:A_{ac}\to A_{ab}\otimes A_{bc},
  $$
  and, for every $a\in S$,
  $$
  \eta_a:k\to A_{aa},\quad \epsilon_a:A_{aa}\to k,\quad
  i_a:C\to A_{aa},\quad i_a^*:A_{aa}\to C.
  $$

These maps obey the following typed equations. The first eight equations are the colored category, unit, coalgebra, counit, and Frobenius laws. The two Frobenius equalities are written separately by their domains and codomains; this avoids chaining opposite-direction composites into one equation.

1. For $a,b,c,d\in S$, associativity is
$$
\mu_{abd}\circ(1_{A_{ab}}\otimes\mu_{bcd})\circ\alpha_{A_{ab},A_{bc},A_{cd}}
=\mu_{acd}\circ(\mu_{abc}\otimes1_{A_{cd}}),
$$
as maps $(A_{ab}\otimes A_{bc})\otimes A_{cd}\to A_{ad}$.

2. The left and right units are
$$
\mu_{aab}\circ(\eta_a\otimes1_{A_{ab}})=\lambda_{A_{ab}},
\qquad
\mu_{abb}\circ(1_{A_{ab}}\otimes\eta_b)=\rho_{A_{ab}}.
$$

3. Coassociativity and the two counits are
$$
\alpha_{A_{ab},A_{bc},A_{cd}}\circ(\Delta_{abc}\otimes1_{A_{cd}})\circ\Delta_{acd}
=(1_{A_{ab}}\otimes\Delta_{bcd})\circ\Delta_{abd},
$$
$$
(\epsilon_a\otimes1_{A_{ab}})\circ\Delta_{aab}=\lambda_{A_{ab}}^{-1},
\qquad
(1_{A_{ab}}\otimes\epsilon_b)\circ\Delta_{abb}=\rho_{A_{ab}}^{-1}.
$$

4. The two typed Frobenius identities are
$$
\Delta_{abd}\circ\mu_{acd}
=(1_{A_{ab}}\otimes\mu_{bcd})\circ\alpha_{A_{ab},A_{bc},A_{cd}}\circ(\Delta_{abc}\otimes1_{A_{cd}}),
$$
as maps $A_{ac}\otimes A_{cd}\to A_{ab}\otimes A_{bd}$, and
$$
\Delta_{acd}\circ\mu_{abd}
=(\mu_{abc}\otimes1_{A_{cd}})\circ\alpha^{-1}_{A_{ab},A_{bc},A_{cd}}\circ(1_{A_{ab}}\otimes\Delta_{bcd}),
$$
as maps $A_{ab}\otimes A_{bd}\to A_{ac}\otimes A_{cd}$.

5. The trace is cyclic across opposite colors:
$$
\epsilon_a\circ\mu_{aba}
=\epsilon_b\circ\mu_{bab}\circ\tau_{A_{ab},A_{ba}}
$$
as maps $A_{ab}\otimes A_{ba}\to k$.

6. Each $i_a$ is a unital algebra map, its image acts centrally on each $A_{ab}$, and $i_a^*$ is pairing-adjoint to $i_a$:
$$
\mu_{aaa}\circ(i_a\otimes i_a)=i_a\circ\mu_C,\qquad
\eta_a=i_a\circ\eta_C,
$$
$$
\mu_{aab}\circ(i_a\otimes1_{A_{ab}})
=\mu_{abb}\circ\tau_{A_{bb},A_{ab}}\circ(i_b\otimes1_{A_{ab}})
$$
as maps $C\otimes A_{ab}\to A_{ab}$, and
$$
\epsilon_C\circ\mu_C\circ(1_C\otimes i_a^*)
=\epsilon_a\circ\mu_{aaa}\circ(i_a\otimes1_{A_{aa}})
$$
as maps $C\otimes A_{aa}\to k$.

7. The colored Cardy equation is
$$
i_a\circ i_b^*
=\mu_{aba}\circ\tau_{A_{ba},A_{ab}}\circ\Delta_{bab}:A_{bb}\to A_{aa}.
$$
In particular, the reverse labels on $A_{ba}$ and $A_{ab}$ are required for the displayed composites to type-check.

A **homomorphism** from unprimed to primed S-colored data is a family of linear maps $f_C:C\to C'$ and $f_{ab}:A_{ab}\to A'_{ab}$ such that $f_C$ preserves the four Frobenius maps on $C$:
$$
\mu'_C(f_C\otimes f_C)=f_C\mu_C,\quad f_C\eta_C=\eta'_C,\quad
\Delta'_C f_C=(f_C\otimes f_C)\Delta_C,\quad
\epsilon'_C f_C=\epsilon_C,
$$
and
$$
\mu'_{abc}(f_{ab}\otimes f_{bc})=f_{ac}\mu_{abc},\quad
f_{aa}\eta_a=\eta'_a,\quad
\Delta'_{abc}f_{ac}=(f_{ab}\otimes f_{bc})\Delta_{abc},
$$
$$
\epsilon'_a f_{aa}=\epsilon_a,\quad
f_{aa}i_a=i'_a f_C,\quad
f_C i_a^*=i_a^{*'}f_{aa}
$$
for all indicated labels. Composition and identities are componentwise. For singleton $S=\{*\}$, write $A=A_{**}$, $i=i_*$, and $i^*=i_*^*$; this is the usual pair $(A,C,i,i^*)$.

For each $a,b\in S$, define the open pairing
$$
b_{ab}:A_{ab}\otimes A_{ba}\to k,\qquad b_{ab}:=\epsilon_a\circ\mu_{aba}.
$$
The cyclic trace equation above identifies $b_{ab}$ with the reversed pairing $b_{ba}\circ\tau_{A_{ab},A_{ba}}$. The equations do not impose nondegeneracy as a separate axiom: [[lem-frobenius-sewing-derived-moves]] proves that both induced maps to algebraic duals are isomorphisms, by exhibiting the two snake composites. For $a=b$, this is the symmetric Frobenius pairing on $A_{aa}$.

No equality $C=Z(A_{aa})$ is part of the definition. The Cardy equation is an additional map equality; it does not identify the underlying vector spaces or force the whole open algebra to be commutative.

In the category $\mathsf{Cob}^{\mathrm{oc}}_2(S)$ of [[def-oriented-open-closed-surface-category]], the ten generator surfaces obey the boundary-relative equalities whose images under a strong symmetric monoidal functor are precisely equations 1–7 in [[def-frobenius-object-and-knowledgeable-sewing-data]]. Thus the closed pair of pants, disk, and reversed pair of pants give a commutative Frobenius object; the open pair of pants, disk, and reversed pair of pants give the indexed open algebra/coalgebra/Frobenius equations and cyclic trace; the zipper and cozipper give the central unital algebra map, pairing adjunction, and colored Cardy equality. Each equality preserves every black parametrization, corner endpoint color, and free-boundary label. This lemma proves the listed relations; it does not assert that they present all surface morphisms.

For the singleton color set, write $A=A_{**}$ and $i=i_*$, $i^*=i^*_*$; then the open pairing is symmetric, while commutativity is required only of $C$.

For S-colored knowledgeable data of [[def-frobenius-object-and-knowledgeable-sewing-data]], all of the following identities follow from its typed equations: open and closed evaluation/coevaluation snakes; symmetry and cyclic invariance of the pairings and their adjoint copairings; both zipper/cozipper pairing and copairing transports; coalgebra and counit preservation by each cozipper; sliding of closed-window and handle operators; the Cardy reduction of an open handle through the closed sector; and cyclic rotation of an open product followed by a cozipper. In particular, define
$$
b_{ab}:=\epsilon_a\mu_{aba}:A_{ab}\otimes A_{ba}\to k,
\qquad d_{ab}:=\Delta_{aba}\eta_a:k\to A_{ab}\otimes A_{ba}.
$$
Both maps to algebraic duals induced by $b_{ab}$ and $b_{ba}$ are isomorphisms. With $b_C=\epsilon_C\mu_C$, $d_C=\Delta_C\eta_C$, $W_a=i_a^*i_a:C\to C$, $H=\mu_C\Delta_C:C\to C$, and $O_a=\mu_{aaa}\Delta_{aaa}:A_{aa}\to A_{aa}$, the typed consequences include
$$
\Delta_Ci_a^*=(i_a^*\otimes i_a^*)\Delta_{aaa},\qquad
\epsilon_Ci_a^*=\epsilon_a,\qquad
i_a^*O_a=W_ai_a^*.
$$
The lemma is algebraic: it assumes the relations already proved in [[lem-elementary-surface-sewing-relations]] and uses no diagram as a proof.

An **equivalence of categories** from $\mathcal C$ to $\mathcal D$ consists of
functors $F:\mathcal C\to\mathcal D$ and $G:\mathcal D\to\mathcal C$, called
**quasi-inverses**, together with natural isomorphisms

$$\eta:1_{\mathcal C}\Rightarrow GF,\qquad \varepsilon:FG\Rightarrow1_{\mathcal D}.$$

The categories are then called **equivalent**. The notions of functor and natural
isomorphism are those of [[def-functor-and-contravariant-functor]] and
[[def-natural-isomorphism]].

An **adjoint equivalence** is such data satisfying the triangle identities

$$G\varepsilon\circ\eta G=1_G,\qquad \varepsilon F\circ F\eta=1_F.$$

Here $G\varepsilon$, $\eta G$, $\varepsilon F$, and $F\eta$ are the
whiskerings of
[[def-horizontal-composition-and-whiskering-of-natural-transformations]].
No triangle identity is required of a bare equivalence.

derivations.claim: Every class in $A$ has a unique form $a+bx$, so $(1,x)$ is a basis, $x^2=0$, and the multiplication is associative as a quotient of $k[x]$. The matrix of $\beta(u,v)=\epsilon(uv)$ in this basis is the displayed matrix; its determinant is $-1$, which is nonzero even in characteristic two. Thus $\beta$ is symmetric and nondegenerate, so $\epsilon$ is a Frobenius functional. The right-dual basis to $(1,x)$ for $\beta$ is $(x,1)$, so the inverse-pairing tensor is $x\otimes1+1\otimes x$. Applying $\Delta(a)=(a\otimes1)(x\otimes1+1\otimes x)$ gives the two formulas.

Direct computation verifies the coalgebra laws. The two counits on $\Delta(1)$ give $\epsilon(1)x+\epsilon(x)1=1$ and $1\epsilon(x)+x\epsilon(1)=1$; on $\Delta(x)$ each gives $x\epsilon(x)=x$. Coassociativity on $1$ gives on both sides
$$
1\otimes x\otimes x+x\otimes1\otimes x+x\otimes x\otimes1,
$$
and on $x$ gives $x\otimes x\otimes x$ on both sides.

To check both Frobenius identities it is enough by bilinearity to use the four ordered basis pairs. For $(1,1)$ both sides are $\Delta(1)$; for $(1,x)$ both sides are $\Delta(x)$; for $(x,1)$ both sides are $x\otimes x$; for $(x,x)$ both sides are $0$, since $x^2=0$. These are exactly $\Delta(ab)=(a\otimes1)\Delta(b)=\Delta(a)(1\otimes b)$, the two typed identities after inserting the vector-space associator. Thus $(A,\mu,\eta,\Delta,\epsilon)$ is a symmetric Frobenius object.

Let $J=kx$. It is a nonzero proper left submodule of $A$, since $x\cdot x=0$ and scalars preserve $J$. If $L\subseteq A$ is any simple left submodule, multiplication by $x$ maps $L$ into $L$. Its image $xL$ is a submodule, so simplicity gives $xL=0$ or $xL=L$. The latter would imply $L=xL=x^2L=0$, contradicting simplicity; hence $xL=0$. For $a+bx\in L$, this implies $0=x(a+bx)=ax$, so $a=0$ and $L\subseteq J$. Therefore every simple submodule of $A$ is contained in the one-dimensional space $J$; their sum cannot equal the two-dimensional module $A$. By [F3], $A$ is not semisimple as a left module over itself.

Fix a field $k$ and write $\mathrm{Vect}_{\mathrm{fd}}(k)$ for finite-dimensional $k$-vector spaces and linear maps, with the algebraic tensor product, unit object $k$, canonical associator $\alpha_{U,V,W}: (U\otimes V)\otimes W\to U\otimes(V\otimes W)$, unitors $\lambda_U:k\otimes U\to U$ and $\rho_U:U\otimes k\to U$, and flip $\tau_{U,V}:U\otimes V\to V\otimes U$. The associator sends $(u\otimes v)\otimes w$ to $u\otimes(v\otimes w)$; the unitors send $c\otimes u$ and $u\otimes c$ to $cu$. All tensor expressions below use these maps, so no strictification is implicit.

A **Frobenius object** in $\mathrm{Vect}_{\mathrm{fd}}(k)$ is a finite-dimensional vector space $A$ and linear maps
$$
\mu:A\otimes A\to A,\qquad \eta:k\to A,\qquad
\Delta:A\to A\otimes A,\qquad \epsilon:A\to k
$$
such that $(A,\mu,\eta)$ is a unital associative algebra, $(A,\Delta,\epsilon)$ is a counital coassociative coalgebra, and the two Frobenius identities hold:
$$
\Delta\circ\mu
=(1_A\otimes\mu)\circ\alpha_{A,A,A}\circ(\Delta\otimes1_A)
=(\mu\otimes1_A)\circ\alpha^{-1}_{A,A,A}\circ(1_A\otimes\Delta).
$$
Here associativity is $\mu\circ(\mu\otimes1_A)=\mu\circ(1_A\otimes\mu)\circ\alpha_{A,A,A}$, and the two unit equations use $\lambda_A,\rho_A$. Coassociativity is $\alpha_{A,A,A}\circ(\Delta\otimes1_A)\circ\Delta=(1_A\otimes\Delta)\circ\Delta$, and the counit equations are $(\epsilon\otimes1_A)\circ\Delta=\lambda_A^{-1}$ and $(1_A\otimes\epsilon)\circ\Delta=\rho_A^{-1}$.

Its **Frobenius pairing** is $b_A:=\epsilon\circ\mu:A\otimes A\to k$. It is **symmetric** when $b_A=b_A\circ\tau_{A,A}$. It is **commutative** when $\mu=\mu\circ\tau_{A,A}$. These are different conditions: commutativity implies symmetry of $b_A$, but symmetry of $b_A$ does not assert commutativity of $\mu$.

An **S-colored knowledgeable Frobenius datum** consists of:

- a commutative Frobenius object $(C,\mu_C,\eta_C,\Delta_C,\epsilon_C)$;
- a finite-dimensional vector space $A_{ab}$ for every ordered pair $a,b\in S$;
- maps, for every $a,b,c\in S$,
  $$
  \mu_{abc}:A_{ab}\otimes A_{bc}\to A_{ac},\quad
  \Delta_{abc}:A_{ac}\to A_{ab}\otimes A_{bc},
  $$
  and, for every $a\in S$,
  $$
  \eta_a:k\to A_{aa},\quad \epsilon_a:A_{aa}\to k,\quad
  i_a:C\to A_{aa},\quad i_a^*:A_{aa}\to C.
  $$

These maps obey the following typed equations. The first eight equations are the colored category, unit, coalgebra, counit, and Frobenius laws. The two Frobenius equalities are written separately by their domains and codomains; this avoids chaining opposite-direction composites into one equation.

1. For $a,b,c,d\in S$, associativity is
$$
\mu_{abd}\circ(1_{A_{ab}}\otimes\mu_{bcd})\circ\alpha_{A_{ab},A_{bc},A_{cd}}
=\mu_{acd}\circ(\mu_{abc}\otimes1_{A_{cd}}),
$$
as maps $(A_{ab}\otimes A_{bc})\otimes A_{cd}\to A_{ad}$.

2. The left and right units are
$$
\mu_{aab}\circ(\eta_a\otimes1_{A_{ab}})=\lambda_{A_{ab}},
\qquad
\mu_{abb}\circ(1_{A_{ab}}\otimes\eta_b)=\rho_{A_{ab}}.
$$

3. Coassociativity and the two counits are
$$
\alpha_{A_{ab},A_{bc},A_{cd}}\circ(\Delta_{abc}\otimes1_{A_{cd}})\circ\Delta_{acd}
=(1_{A_{ab}}\otimes\Delta_{bcd})\circ\Delta_{abd},
$$
$$
(\epsilon_a\otimes1_{A_{ab}})\circ\Delta_{aab}=\lambda_{A_{ab}}^{-1},
\qquad
(1_{A_{ab}}\otimes\epsilon_b)\circ\Delta_{abb}=\rho_{A_{ab}}^{-1}.
$$

4. The two typed Frobenius identities are
$$
\Delta_{abd}\circ\mu_{acd}
=(1_{A_{ab}}\otimes\mu_{bcd})\circ\alpha_{A_{ab},A_{bc},A_{cd}}\circ(\Delta_{abc}\otimes1_{A_{cd}}),
$$
as maps $A_{ac}\otimes A_{cd}\to A_{ab}\otimes A_{bd}$, and
$$
\Delta_{acd}\circ\mu_{abd}
=(\mu_{abc}\otimes1_{A_{cd}})\circ\alpha^{-1}_{A_{ab},A_{bc},A_{cd}}\circ(1_{A_{ab}}\otimes\Delta_{bcd}),
$$
as maps $A_{ab}\otimes A_{bd}\to A_{ac}\otimes A_{cd}$.

5. The trace is cyclic across opposite colors:
$$
\epsilon_a\circ\mu_{aba}
=\epsilon_b\circ\mu_{bab}\circ\tau_{A_{ab},A_{ba}}
$$
as maps $A_{ab}\otimes A_{ba}\to k$.

6. Each $i_a$ is a unital algebra map, its image acts centrally on each $A_{ab}$, and $i_a^*$ is pairing-adjoint to $i_a$:
$$
\mu_{aaa}\circ(i_a\otimes i_a)=i_a\circ\mu_C,\qquad
\eta_a=i_a\circ\eta_C,
$$
$$
\mu_{aab}\circ(i_a\otimes1_{A_{ab}})
=\mu_{abb}\circ\tau_{A_{bb},A_{ab}}\circ(i_b\otimes1_{A_{ab}})
$$
as maps $C\otimes A_{ab}\to A_{ab}$, and
$$
\epsilon_C\circ\mu_C\circ(1_C\otimes i_a^*)
=\epsilon_a\circ\mu_{aaa}\circ(i_a\otimes1_{A_{aa}})
$$
as maps $C\otimes A_{aa}\to k$.

7. The colored Cardy equation is
$$
i_a\circ i_b^*
=\mu_{aba}\circ\tau_{A_{ba},A_{ab}}\circ\Delta_{bab}:A_{bb}\to A_{aa}.
$$
In particular, the reverse labels on $A_{ba}$ and $A_{ab}$ are required for the displayed composites to type-check.

A **homomorphism** from unprimed to primed S-colored data is a family of linear maps $f_C:C\to C'$ and $f_{ab}:A_{ab}\to A'_{ab}$ such that $f_C$ preserves the four Frobenius maps on $C$:
$$
\mu'_C(f_C\otimes f_C)=f_C\mu_C,\quad f_C\eta_C=\eta'_C,\quad
\Delta'_C f_C=(f_C\otimes f_C)\Delta_C,\quad
\epsilon'_C f_C=\epsilon_C,
$$
and
$$
\mu'_{abc}(f_{ab}\otimes f_{bc})=f_{ac}\mu_{abc},\quad
f_{aa}\eta_a=\eta'_a,\quad
\Delta'_{abc}f_{ac}=(f_{ab}\otimes f_{bc})\Delta_{abc},
$$
$$
\epsilon'_a f_{aa}=\epsilon_a,\quad
f_{aa}i_a=i'_a f_C,\quad
f_C i_a^*=i_a^{*'}f_{aa}
$$
for all indicated labels. Composition and identities are componentwise. For singleton $S=\{*\}$, write $A=A_{**}$, $i=i_*$, and $i^*=i_*^*$; this is the usual pair $(A,C,i,i^*)$.

For each $a,b\in S$, define the open pairing
$$
b_{ab}:A_{ab}\otimes A_{ba}\to k,\qquad b_{ab}:=\epsilon_a\circ\mu_{aba}.
$$
The cyclic trace equation above identifies $b_{ab}$ with the reversed pairing $b_{ba}\circ\tau_{A_{ab},A_{ba}}$. The equations do not impose nondegeneracy as a separate axiom: [[lem-frobenius-sewing-derived-moves]] proves that both induced maps to algebraic duals are isomorphisms, by exhibiting the two snake composites. For $a=b$, this is the symmetric Frobenius pairing on $A_{aa}$.

No equality $C=Z(A_{aa})$ is part of the definition. The Cardy equation is an additional map equality; it does not identify the underlying vector spaces or force the whole open algebra to be commutative.

Let $k$ be any field, let $A$ be a finite-dimensional unital associative $k$-algebra, and let $\epsilon:A\to k$ be a Frobenius functional, so $\beta(a,b):=\epsilon(ab)$ is nondegenerate in both variables. Then there is a unique tensor
$$
e=\sum_i x_i\otimes y_i\in A\otimes A
$$
such that, for every $a\in A$,
$$
\sum_i\epsilon(a x_i)y_i=a
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\sum_i x_i\epsilon(y_i a)=a.
$$
It is independent of the basis used to construct it and satisfies
$$
(a\otimes1)e=e(1\otimes a).
$$
The map $\Delta:A\to A\otimes A$ defined by $\Delta(a):=(a\otimes1)e$ is coassociative, has counit $\epsilon$, and satisfies both Frobenius identities. Conversely, every finite-dimensional Frobenius object $(A,\mu,\eta,\Delta,\epsilon)$ in $\mathrm{Vect}_{\mathrm{fd}}(k)$ has nondegenerate functional pairing $\epsilon(ab)$, and this $\Delta$ is the unique coproduct with that counit and Frobenius identities.

Symmetry of $\beta$ is not assumed. If it holds, the Frobenius object is symmetric; if $\mu$ is commutative, then $\beta$ is symmetric, but neither condition is identified with the other.
A left $R$-module is **semisimple** when it is an internal direct sum of simple submodules, allowing the empty direct sum. Hence the zero module is semisimple.

A left $R$-module $M$ is **simple** if $M\ne0$ and its only submodules are
$0$ and $M$. Equivalently, $M\ne0$ and $M$ has no proper nonzero submodule.

derivations.claim:
Apply [F2] to $G=S_3$. It gives the symmetric nondegenerate associative form $\langle x,y\rangle=$ coefficient of $[e]$ in $xy$; by the Frobenius definition this makes $k[S_3]$ a symmetric Frobenius algebra over any field. In $S_3$, $(12)(23)=(123)$ and $(23)(12)=(132)$ under the stated composition convention. These permutations are distinct, and their corresponding group elements are distinct basis vectors by [F1]. Therefore
$$
[(12)][(23)]=[(123)]\ne[(132)]=[(23)][(12)],
$$
so the multiplication is not commutative.

If this algebra were itself assigned to the circle by a closed oriented two-dimensional TQFT, [F3] would make its multiplication commutative, contradicting step 1.1. Hence it is not a closed sector of that form. The argument concerns only the closed circle object; it neither constructs nor rules out a separate open/closed extension with a different commutative closed algebra.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring ([[def-commutative-ring]]) and let $G$ be a group
([[def-group]]). The **group ring** $R[G]$ is the free left $R$-module on the
set $G$ ([[def-free-module-on-a-set-and-standard-basis]]).

For each $g \in G$, write $[g] \in R[G]$ for the standard basis vector indexed
by $g$. Thus every element of $R[G]$ has a unique expression
$$\sum_{g \in F} r_g [g]$$
with $F \subseteq G$ finite and $r_g \in R$.

The notation is deliberately that of **formal** finite sums: at this stage
$R[G]$ is only the underlying free $R$-module with its distinguished basis. The
multiplication satisfying
$$[g][h]=[gh]$$
and the resulting $R$-algebra structure are constructed in
[[thm-group-ring-is-a-unital-algebra-with-basis-g]].

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $G$ be a group. Write $[g] \in R[G]$ for
the basis vector of [[def-group-ring]] indexed by $g \in G$.

There is a unique $R$-bilinear multiplication on $R[G]$ satisfying
$$[g][h]=[gh]\qquad(g,h\in G).$$
With this product, $R[G]$ is a unital $R$-algebra whose underlying
$R$-module has basis $\{[g]:g\in G\}$. Its identity is $[e]$, where $e$ is the
identity of $G$, and every basis element $[g]$ is a unit with inverse
$[g^{-1}]$.

Let $G$ be a finite group and $k$ a field. The bilinear form

$$ \langle x,y\rangle:=\text{the coefficient of }[e]\text{ in }xy $$

on the group algebra $k[G]$ is associative, symmetric, and nondegenerate.
Hence $k[G]$ is a symmetric Frobenius algebra.

For any field $k$, the category of strong symmetric monoidal functors $\mathsf{Cob}^{\mathrm{cl}}_2\to\mathrm{Vect}_{\mathrm{fd}}(k)$ and monoidal natural transformations is equivalent to the category of finite-dimensional commutative Frobenius $k$-algebras and maps preserving multiplication, unit, comultiplication, and counit. Here $\mathsf{Cob}^{\mathrm{cl}}_2$ has circle words as objects and only surfaces with **no free boundary at all** as morphisms. It is not the full subcategory on circle objects inside the open-closed category, since that larger category also has circle-to-circle morphisms with free windows.

If $M$ is connected with genus $g$, $m$ incoming circles and $n$ outgoing circles, its value under the functor corresponding to $(C,\mu,\eta,\Delta,\epsilon)$ is
$$
\Delta_C^{[n]}\circ H^g\circ\mu_C^{[m]}:C^{\otimes m}\to C^{\otimes n},
\qquad H:=\mu_C\Delta_C,
$$
where $\mu_C^{[0]}=\eta_C$, $\Delta_C^{[0]}=\epsilon_C$, and $\mu_C^{[1]}=\Delta_C^{[1]}=1_C$. Disconnected surfaces are evaluated by tensor products and the boundary-slot symmetries.
